text:
Before you start
In this session you’ll describe a dataset of 60 patients who were tested for COVID-19. For each patient it records their age and sex, their test result, and four laboratory and clinical measurements: white blood cell count (WBC, × 109/L), C-reactive protein (CRP, mg/L), systolic blood pressure (BP_Sys, mmHg) and total cholesterol (mmol/L). The data are simulated.
The aim is to describe the data accurately, in numbers, tables and graphs. Whether any differences you see are bigger than chance would produce is a question for week 4, so for now: describe what you see, not what you expected to see.
Keep the Guide to R 04 open alongside. Make sure this workbook and covid_stats.csv are in your R_module project, and that the project is open.

title: Week 2, session 2: before the session
text: Before you test anything, you describe it: how big a typical value is, how much the values vary, and what shape they make. In session 2 you’ll describe a dataset of patients tested for COVID-19, in numbers, in a table and in graphs. This page covers the ideas you’ll need:

title: Week 2, session 2: before the session
section: 1. The mean, the median, and one extreme value
text:
1. The mean, the median, and one extreme value
Here are the C-reactive protein (CRP) results of seven patients, in mg/L. CRP is a marker of inflammation; in a healthy person it’s usually below about 5 mg/L.








The mean adds up the values and divides by how many there are. Six of the seven patients have a CRP between 4 and 15 mg/L, but the mean is over 50, because the one patient with 310 mg/L pulls it up. The mean is not a good description of a “typical” patient here.
The median is the middle value when the values are sorted: half are below it and half above. A single extreme value doesn’t move it, because it only cares about the order.

Your turn
Calculate the median of crp. (The function is called exactly what you’d guess.)





















NoteHint





The function is median().











TipSolution





median(crp)




When the mean and the median are close, the values are roughly symmetric. When the mean is much bigger than the median, a few high values are stretching the distribution to the right: it is right-skewed. Many biomarkers behave like this, and for them the median is usually the better summary.

title: Week 2, session 2: before the session
text:
2. Spread: the standard deviation
Two groups can have the same mean and still be very different. The standard deviation (SD) measures how spread out the values are: roughly, the typical distance of a value from the mean.








Both groups have a mean of 50, but group B’s values are far more spread out, and its SD is ten times larger. When the data are skewed, the interquartile range (IQR, the range of the middle half of the values) does the same job for the median that the SD does for the mean: IQR(crp).

title: Week 2, session 2: before the session
text:
3. Summaries for each group
summarise() reduces a whole column to a few summary numbers. Put group_by() in front of it, and you get the same summaries for every group. Using ToothGrowth again (the guinea pigs given vitamin C as orange juice, OJ, or ascorbic acid, VC), here is the number of animals and the mean tooth length at each dose:








Read it as: “take ToothGrowth, and then split it into groups by dose, and then calculate, for each group, the number of rows and the mean of len”. The names on the left of each = become the column names of the result.

Your turn
Calculate the mean tooth length for each supplement (supp) instead of each dose. Call the column mean_len.






















NoteHint





The grouping column is supp, and the summary is mean(len), just as in the example.











TipSolution





ToothGrowth |>
  group_by(supp) |>
  summarise(mean_len = mean(len))

title: Week 2, session 2: before the session
text:
4. Seeing the shape: histograms
Numbers like the mean and SD summarise a distribution; a histogram shows it. It divides the range of values into bins and draws a bar for the number of values in each bin. You only need to give it an x:








binwidth = 2 makes each bar 2 units wide. fill and colour are fixed settings for the inside and the outline of the bars, so they go outside aes(). #753bbd is a hex code for a shade of purple.

Your turn
Draw a histogram of tooth length with wider bins, 5 units each. Does the shape look different?


















NoteHint





Replace the blank with the number 5.











TipSolution





ggplot(ToothGrowth, aes(x = len)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "#753bbd", colour = "white")






Which graph?
Each type of graph answers a different kind of question. Decide which you would use for each question below, then open the box to check.

How are patients’ cholesterol levels distributed?
Does systolic blood pressure differ between three treatment groups?
Is there a relationship between age and white cell count?
How many patients in each group are smokers?
How does mean HbA1c change over the six months of a trial?







TipAnswers






A histogram: the distribution of one continuous variable.
Boxplots, one per group: a continuous variable compared across groups.
A scatter plot: two continuous variables, one point per patient.
A bar chart of counts: a categorical variable.
A line graph: change over time.

title: Guide to R 03: Tidy data and wrangling
text:
Tidy data, and clean data
Before any analysis, a dataset has to be both tidy and clean. The two words mean different things.
Tidy is about shape. A tidy dataset follows three rules:

each variable has its own column;
each observation has its own row; and
each value has its own cell.

Clean is about content: every category is spelled one way, numbers are stored as numbers, missing results are recorded as missing rather than as a made-up number, and nobody appears twice by accident.
Spreadsheets break both sets of rules all the time, usually for good reasons: a layout that is easy to type into is often not the layout R needs. The skill you’re learning this week is getting from one to the other in code, so that every change is recorded and can be repeated.






ImportantNever edit the raw data file



It is tempting to open the CSV in Excel and fix things by hand. Don’t. A hand edit leaves no record of what was changed, can’t be repeated when new data arrives, and is easy to get wrong without noticing (Excel, for example, silently turns some gene names into dates). Keep the original file exactly as you received it, and do every fix in your code. If you make a mistake, you can always start again from the raw file.

title: Guide to R 03: Tidy data and wrangling
section: A routine for cleaning any dataset
text:
A routine for cleaning any dataset
The order below works for almost every dataset you will meet. The rest of this guide follows it.

Import, and look. glimpse(), summary() and count() on every categorical column.
Tidy the column names. clean_names(), then rename() where needed.
Fix the types. Numbers stored as text: as.numeric() or parse_number().
Fix the categories. One spelling per category: case_when(), then factor().
Deal with missing values. Find codes such as -99 and turn them into NA; then decide how to handle the NAs.
Remove accidental duplicates. distinct().
Change the shape if you need to. pivot_longer() and pivot_wider().
Check after every step, then save a clean copy under a new name.

title: Guide to R 03: Tidy data and wrangling
text:
Packages for this session
Everything here comes from the tidyverse except clean_names(), which is in the janitor package. Install janitor once, in the Console:

install.packages("janitor")

Then load both at the top of your workbook or script:

library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)

The tidyverse includes stringr, for working with text (its functions all start str_), and tidyr, for changing the shape of a table. You don’t need to load them separately.

title: Guide to R 03: Tidy data and wrangling
text:
Step 1: Import, and look
Import the file and keep it under a name that makes clear it is untouched. Every cleaning step will then build a new object from it.

patients_raw <- read_csv("data/Dataset.csv")

Rows: 5 Columns: 7
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (5): Patient_ID, Sex, CRP_mg.L, COVID_Result, FollowUp_Required
dbl (2): Age, WBC_Count_10^9.L

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

patients_raw

# A tibble: 5 × 7
  Patient_ID   Age Sex    CRP_mg.L `WBC_Count_10^9.L` COVID_Result  
  <chr>      <dbl> <chr>  <chr>                 <dbl> <chr>         
1 P001          45 M      12.5                    8.4 "Positive"    
2 P002          38 F      8.1                     7.2 "positive"    
3 P003          52 male   <NA>                    6.9 "NEG"         
4 P004          29 Female 5.3                    NA   "\"negative\""
5 P005          NA M      High                   10.2 "Pos"         
# ℹ 1 more variable: FollowUp_Required <chr>


With five rows you can see everything at once. With hundreds you can’t, and you need tools that summarise each column for you. glimpse() and summary() (from week 1) show each column’s type and range. For a categorical column, the most useful tool is count(), which lists every distinct value and how many rows have it:

patients_raw |> count(Sex)

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  Sex        n
  <chr>  <int>
1 F          1
2 Female     1
3 M          2
4 male       1

patients_raw |> count(COVID_Result)

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  COVID_Result       n
  <chr>          <int>
1 "\"negative\""     1
2 "NEG"              1
3 "Pos"              1
4 "Positive"         1
5 "positive"         1

patients_raw |> count(FollowUp_Required)

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  FollowUp_Required     n
  <chr>             <int>
1 No                    1
2 T                     1
3 Y                     1
4 Yes                   1
5 n                     1


Every distinct spelling is a separate category as far as R is concerned. Sex should have two categories and has four; COVID_Result should have two and has five, one of which ("negative") has quotation marks stored inside the value; and FollowUp_Required includes a T, which might mean “true” or might be a typing slip.







Code
What it does




patients_raw |>
Takes the raw data and then passes it to the next function.


count(Sex)
Counts the rows for each distinct value of Sex. The result is a small tibble: one row per value, and a column n holding the counts.



It also pays to count the missing values in every column:

colSums(is.na(patients_raw))

       Patient_ID               Age               Sex          CRP_mg.L 
                0                 1                 0                 1 
 WBC_Count_10^9.L      COVID_Result FollowUp_Required 
                1                 0                 0 









Code
What it does




is.na(patients_raw)
Checks every cell, giving TRUE where the value is missing and FALSE where it isn’t.


colSums(...)
Adds up each column. TRUE counts as 1 and FALSE as 0, so the total is the number of missing values in that column.



read_csv() turns empty cells and cells containing NA into missing values automatically, so P003’s CRP and P004’s white cell count are already NA. Notice what isn’t counted: P005’s CRP is recorded as “High”, which is not missing, just not a number. We’ll come back to it in Step 3.

title: Guide to R 03: Tidy data and wrangling
text:
Step 2: Tidy the column names
The column names in this file use a mixture of styles (Patient_ID, CRP_mg.L, FollowUp_Required), and one contains a ^, which isn’t allowed in an R name. clean_names() converts every name to the same style in one go:

patients <- patients_raw |> clean_names()

tibble(before = names(patients_raw), after = names(patients))

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  before            after             
  <chr>             <chr>             
1 Patient_ID        patient_id        
2 Age               age               
3 Sex               sex               
4 CRP_mg.L          crp_mg_l          
5 WBC_Count_10^9.L  wbc_count_10_9_l  
6 COVID_Result      covid_result      
7 FollowUp_Required follow_up_required


Every name is now in lower case; anything that isn’t a letter or a number has become an underscore; and words that were run together with capital letters have been split (FollowUp has become follow_up). This style is called snake case, and it’s the one used throughout the tidyverse.







Code
What it does




patients <-
Stores the result in a new object, patients. patients_raw is left exactly as it was.


patients_raw |> clean_names()
Takes the raw data and gives back the same data with tidied column names.


tibble(before = ..., after = ...)
Builds a small two-column table so that the old and new names can be compared side by side.



clean_names() fixes the style of the names, but it can’t make them short or meaningful. wbc_count_10_9_l is legal but tedious to type, so give it a better name with rename(). The new name goes on the left of the =, and the existing name on the right:

patients <- patients |> rename(wbc = wbc_count_10_9_l)
names(patients)

[1] "patient_id"         "age"                "sex"               
[4] "crp_mg_l"           "wbc"                "covid_result"      
[7] "follow_up_required"








TipKeep the units somewhere



Short names lose information: wbc doesn’t tell a reader that the values are × 109/L. Put the units in your axis labels and table headings, and in a note at the top of your script.

title: Guide to R 03: Tidy data and wrangling
text:
Step 3: Numbers stored as text
You met this problem in week 1: one entry of “High” was enough to make R read the whole CRP column as text. as.numeric() converts it to numbers, and anything that isn’t a number becomes NA, with a warning:

patients <- patients |> mutate(crp_mg_l = as.numeric(crp_mg_l))

Warning: There was 1 warning in `mutate()`.
ℹ In argument: `crp_mg_l = as.numeric(crp_mg_l)`.
Caused by warning:
! NAs introduced by coercion


Read that warning, and decide whether you are happy with what it describes. Here, P005’s CRP was presumably high enough to be off the scale of the analyser, so turning it into “unknown” throws away real information. In a write-up you would say what you did and why.
A different version of the same problem is a number with text stuck to it: "63 yrs" rather than 63. as.numeric() would turn every one of those into NA. parse_number() (from the readr package) is smarter: it finds the first number in each value and drops the text around it.

ages <- c("54", "63 yrs", "72 years", "about 40")
as.numeric(ages)

Warning: NAs introduced by coercion


[1] 54 NA NA NA

parse_number(ages)

[1] 54 63 72 40


parse_number() is very helpful, but it does exactly what it says and no more. It would turn "2 to 3 days" into 2, and "<0.5" into 0.5, without any warning. Always look at the values you’re converting before you trust the result.

title: Guide to R 03: Tidy data and wrangling
text:
Step 4: One spelling per category

Recoding with case_when()
case_when() goes inside mutate() and works through a set of rules in order. Each rule has a condition, a tilde (~, read it as “then”) and the value to use:

patients <- patients |>
  mutate(
    sex = str_to_lower(sex),
    sex = case_when(
      sex %in% c("m", "male") ~ "Male",
      sex %in% c("f", "female") ~ "Female"
    )
  )

patients |> count(sex)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  sex        n
  <chr>  <int>
1 Female     2
2 Male       3









Code
What it does




mutate(
Changes or creates columns. Each line inside is one change, and they happen in order.


sex = str_to_lower(sex),
Converts every value of sex to lower case, so “Female” becomes “female” and “M” becomes “m”. This halves the number of spellings the next step has to handle.


sex = case_when(
Replaces sex with the result of the rules that follow.


sex %in% c("m", "male") ~ "Male",
If the value is one of “m” or “male”, then use “Male”.


sex %in% c("f", "female") ~ "Female"
If it is “f” or “female”, then use “Female”.


patients |> count(sex)
Checks the result. Two categories, adding up to five patients, means every value matched a rule.



Any value that matches no rule becomes NA. That is a safety feature: if a spelling turns up that you didn’t expect (say, “fem”), it appears as NA in your count() instead of being quietly put in the wrong group. This is why every recode should be followed by a count().
COVID_Result needs one extra step, because one value has quotation marks stored inside it. str_remove_all() deletes every copy of a piece of text; here, the piece of text is a double quotation mark, which has to be written inside single quotation marks, '"':

patients <- patients |>
  mutate(
    covid_result = str_to_lower(covid_result),
    covid_result = str_remove_all(covid_result, '"'),
    covid_result = case_when(
      covid_result %in% c("positive", "pos") ~ "Positive",
      covid_result %in% c("negative", "neg") ~ "Negative"
    )
  )

patients |> count(covid_result)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  covid_result     n
  <chr>        <int>
1 Negative         2
2 Positive         3




When a value can’t be recoded with confidence
follow_up_required contains “Yes”, “Y”, “No”, “n” and “T”. The first four are clear. “T” is not: it might mean “true”, or it might be a slip of the finger. The honest thing to do is to leave it out of the rules, so that it becomes NA, and record the decision:

patients <- patients |>
  mutate(
    follow_up_required = case_when(
      follow_up_required %in% c("Yes", "Y") ~ "Yes",
      follow_up_required %in% c("No", "n") ~ "No"
      # "T" is ambiguous, so it is deliberately left to become NA
    )
  )

patients |> count(follow_up_required)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  follow_up_required     n
  <chr>              <int>
1 No                     2
2 Yes                    2
3 <NA>                   1


If you can check the original record, do. If you can’t, a missing value is better than a guess that nobody knows was a guess.


Factors
A factor is R’s way of storing a categorical variable with a fixed set of categories, called levels. Statistical tests and plots treat factors as groups, and the order of the levels decides the order in which groups appear in tables and on plot axes. (In regression, later in the module, the first level is also the reference group that the others are compared with.) Unless you say otherwise, R puts the levels in alphabetical order. To choose the order yourself, list the levels:

patients <- patients |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c("Female", "Male")),
    covid_result = factor(covid_result, levels = c("Negative", "Positive"))
  )

glimpse(patients)

Rows: 5
Columns: 7
$ patient_id         <chr> "P001", "P002", "P003", "P004", "P005"
$ age                <dbl> 45, 38, 52, 29, NA
$ sex                <fct> Male, Female, Male, Female, Male
$ crp_mg_l           <dbl> 12.5, 8.1, NA, 5.3, NA
$ wbc                <dbl> 8.4, 7.2, 6.9, NA, 10.2
$ covid_result       <fct> Positive, Positive, Negative, Negative, Positive
$ follow_up_required <chr> "Yes", "Yes", "No", "No", NA


glimpse() now shows sex and covid_result as <fct>. factor() can also replace short codes with readable labels at the same time. The levels are the values as they appear in the data, and the labels are what you want to see instead, in the same order:

data <- data |>
  mutate(group = factor(group,
                        levels = c("UC", "ILP"),
                        labels = c("Usual care", "Intensive lifestyle")))

You’ll use exactly this in the workbook.

title: Guide to R 03: Tidy data and wrangling
text:
Step 5: Missing values

NA in calculations
R’s symbol for a missing value is NA (“not available”). Most calculations involving an NA give NA, because if one value is unknown, the answer is strictly unknown too:

mean(patients$age)

[1] NA

mean(patients$age, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 41


na.rm = TRUE (“NA remove: yes”) tells the function to use the values it has. That’s usually what you want, but it means the answer is based on fewer observations, so report how many: sum(!is.na(patients$age)) counts the values that are not missing (! means “not”).


Codes that mean “missing”
Some datasets use a number such as -99, 999 or 9999 to mean “no result”. R has no way of knowing that, so it treats the code as a real measurement, with dramatic effects on means, ranges and plots:

lab <- tibble(glucose = c(5.4, 6.1, -99, 5.8, 999, 6.4))
lab |> summarise(mean_glucose = mean(glucose))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  mean_glucose
         <dbl>
1         154.


The clue is usually in summary(): a minimum or maximum that is biologically impossible. if_else() swaps the codes for NA:

lab <- lab |>
  mutate(glucose = if_else(glucose %in% c(-99, 999), NA, glucose))

lab |> summarise(mean_glucose = mean(glucose, na.rm = TRUE))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  mean_glucose
         <dbl>
1         5.92









Code
What it does




if_else(
Chooses between two values for every row, depending on a condition.


glucose %in% c(-99, 999),
The condition: is the value one of the codes?


NA,
The value to use where the condition is TRUE.


glucose)
The value to use where it is FALSE: the original value, unchanged.



If you already know the codes before you import, read_csv() can turn them into NA as it reads the file: read_csv("data/file.csv", na = c("", "NA", "-99", "999")). Be careful, though: this applies to every column, so it would also wipe out a genuine 999 anywhere else in the file.


Deciding what to do with missing values
Once the missing values are recorded as NA, you have to decide how to handle them. There are two common approaches.
Removing rows with missing values, also called complete-case analysis:

patients |> drop_na() # rows with no missing values at all

# A tibble: 2 × 7
  patient_id   age sex    crp_mg_l   wbc covid_result follow_up_required
  <chr>      <dbl> <fct>     <dbl> <dbl> <fct>        <chr>             
1 P001          45 Male       12.5   8.4 Positive     Yes               
2 P002          38 Female      8.1   7.2 Positive     Yes               

patients |> drop_na(age) # rows where age, specifically, isn't missing

# A tibble: 4 × 7
  patient_id   age sex    crp_mg_l   wbc covid_result follow_up_required
  <chr>      <dbl> <fct>     <dbl> <dbl> <fct>        <chr>             
1 P001          45 Male       12.5   8.4 Positive     Yes               
2 P002          38 Female      8.1   7.2 Positive     Yes               
3 P003          52 Male       NA     6.9 Negative     No                
4 P004          29 Female      5.3  NA   Negative     No                


drop_na() with nothing in the brackets keeps only the rows with no missing values anywhere: here, just two of the five patients. Naming a column, as in drop_na(age), removes only the rows where that column is missing, which usually loses far less.
Removing rows is quick, and many functions need complete data. But it can throw away a lot: in biomedical datasets, missing values are common, and a few in each of several columns can remove most of the rows. More seriously, if the missingness isn’t random (for example, if the sickest patients are the ones least likely to complete their tests), removing those patients biases the results. So complete-case analysis is reasonable only when few values are missing, the missingness is plausibly random, and the analysis doesn’t need every last observation.
Replacing missing values with a stand-in value, a simple form of imputation:

patients |> mutate(age = replace_na(age, mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)))

# A tibble: 5 × 7
  patient_id   age sex    crp_mg_l   wbc covid_result follow_up_required
  <chr>      <dbl> <fct>     <dbl> <dbl> <fct>        <chr>             
1 P001          45 Male       12.5   8.4 Positive     Yes               
2 P002          38 Female      8.1   7.2 Positive     Yes               
3 P003          52 Male       NA     6.9 Negative     No                
4 P004          29 Female      5.3  NA   Negative     No                
5 P005          41 Male       NA    10.2 Positive     <NA>              


This keeps every row, but it must be done carefully. Filling gaps with the mean makes the data look less variable than it really is, and can hide real patterns. Replacing every missing CRP with the average, for instance, ignores the fact that CRP is often only measured in patients who are unwell. If you do impute, choose a value that makes sense in context, document and justify it, and consider adding a column that flags which values were imputed. More sophisticated methods exist (and are beyond this module), but the principle is the same.


Why the data is missing matters more than how much
The right approach depends on why values are missing. There are three broad types:

Missing completely at random (MCAR): missingness is unrelated to anything, such as a sample dropped on the floor. Removing or imputing is unlikely to introduce bias.
Missing at random (MAR): missingness depends on something you have measured, such as older patients being less likely to attend follow-up.
Missing not at random (MNAR): missingness depends on the missing value itself, such as patients with the most severe illness not returning for blood tests.

You can’t usually prove which applies from the data alone; it needs knowledge of how the data were collected. Whatever you decide, the rule is the same: explore the missing values first, make the decision deliberately, and report what you did.

title: Guide to R 03: Tidy data and wrangling
text:
Step 6: Duplicate rows
The file covid.csv is a small dataset in which some patients have been entered twice:

covid <- read_csv("data/covid.csv")

Rows: 8 Columns: 6
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (3): Patient_ID, Sex, COVID_Result
dbl (3): Age, CRP_mg.L, WBC

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

covid

# A tibble: 8 × 6
  Patient_ID   Age Sex   CRP_mg.L   WBC COVID_Result
  <chr>      <dbl> <chr>    <dbl> <dbl> <chr>       
1 P001          45 M         12.5   8.4 Positive    
2 P002          38 F          8.1   7.2 Positive    
3 P003          52 M          7.4   6.9 Negative    
4 P004          29 F          5.3   6.2 Negative    
5 P003          52 M          7.4   6.9 Negative    
6 P005          60 M          9     7.5 Positive    
7 P002          38 F          8.1   7.2 Positive    
8 P006          34 F          6.1   5.8 Negative    


In eight rows the repeats are easy to spot by eye; in a large dataset they aren’t. Counting how many rows each patient ID has, then keeping the IDs with more than one, finds them:

covid |> count(Patient_ID) |> filter(n > 1)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  Patient_ID     n
  <chr>      <int>
1 P002           2
2 P003           2


distinct() removes rows that are exact copies of an earlier row:

covid_clean <- covid |> distinct()
covid_clean

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  Patient_ID   Age Sex   CRP_mg.L   WBC COVID_Result
  <chr>      <dbl> <chr>    <dbl> <dbl> <chr>       
1 P001          45 M         12.5   8.4 Positive    
2 P002          38 F          8.1   7.2 Positive    
3 P003          52 M          7.4   6.9 Negative    
4 P004          29 F          5.3   6.2 Negative    
5 P005          60 M          9     7.5 Positive    
6 P006          34 F          6.1   5.8 Negative    


distinct() only removes rows that are identical in every column. If the same patient ID appears twice with different values, that’s a different problem: two different results, or two different patients given the same ID by mistake. Investigate it rather than deleting one of them.

title: Guide to R 03: Tidy data and wrangling
text:
Step 7: Wide and long

From wide to long
Here are four patients’ systolic blood pressures, measured at the start of a study and again after 12 weeks:

bp_wide <- tibble(
  patient = c("P01", "P02", "P03", "P04"),
  treatment = c("Drug", "Placebo", "Drug", "Placebo"),
  sbp_baseline = c(148, 135, 160, 142),
  sbp_week_12 = c(136, 133, 145, 141)
)
bp_wide

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  patient treatment sbp_baseline sbp_week_12
  <chr>   <chr>            <dbl>       <dbl>
1 P01     Drug               148         136
2 P02     Placebo            135         133
3 P03     Drug               160         145
4 P04     Placebo            142         141


This is wide format: one row per patient, with the measurements at different times in different columns. It’s the natural way to type data in, but it isn’t tidy: “timepoint” is a variable, and it is hidden in the column names. Long format gives each measurement its own row, with the timepoint in a column of its own. pivot_longer() does the conversion:

bp_long <- bp_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(sbp_baseline, sbp_week_12),
    names_to = "timepoint",
    values_to = "sbp"
  )
bp_long

# A tibble: 8 × 4
  patient treatment timepoint      sbp
  <chr>   <chr>     <chr>        <dbl>
1 P01     Drug      sbp_baseline   148
2 P01     Drug      sbp_week_12    136
3 P02     Placebo   sbp_baseline   135
4 P02     Placebo   sbp_week_12    133
5 P03     Drug      sbp_baseline   160
6 P03     Drug      sbp_week_12    145
7 P04     Placebo   sbp_baseline   142
8 P04     Placebo   sbp_week_12    141









Code
What it does




pivot_longer(
Stacks several columns into two.


cols = c(sbp_baseline, sbp_week_12),
The columns to stack. Every other column (patient, treatment) is repeated on each new row.


names_to = "timepoint",
The name of the new column that holds the old column names. It’s in quotation marks because it doesn’t exist yet.


values_to = "sbp"
The name of the new column that holds the values.



Four patients × two timepoints = eight rows. Two quick tips: if the columns to stack share a beginning, cols = starts_with("sbp") saves typing; and you can tidy up the timepoint labels, and fix their order, with factor(), exactly as in Step 4:

bp_long <- bp_long |>
  mutate(timepoint = factor(timepoint,
                            levels = c("sbp_baseline", "sbp_week_12"),
                            labels = c("Baseline", "Week 12")))
bp_long

# A tibble: 8 × 4
  patient treatment timepoint   sbp
  <chr>   <chr>     <fct>     <dbl>
1 P01     Drug      Baseline    148
2 P01     Drug      Week 12     136
3 P02     Placebo   Baseline    135
4 P02     Placebo   Week 12     133
5 P03     Drug      Baseline    160
6 P03     Drug      Week 12     145
7 P04     Placebo   Baseline    142
8 P04     Placebo   Week 12     141


Without the levels, R would put text labels in alphabetical order. That happens to work here, but it wouldn’t for labels such as “Baseline”, “3 months” and “6 months”, where alphabetical order would put “Baseline” last.


Why long format helps
Most tidyverse functions expect long data. A plot of each patient’s change over time, for example, needs the timepoint in one column and the blood pressure in another:

ggplot(bp_long, aes(x = timepoint, y = sbp, group = patient, colour = treatment)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Drug = "#753bbd", Placebo = "#b48fe0")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Systolic blood pressure (mmHg)", colour = "Treatment") +
  theme_minimal()















Code
What it does




aes(x = timepoint, y = sbp, ...)
Puts the timepoint on the x axis and blood pressure on the y axis.


group = patient
Tells ggplot which points belong together, so geom_line() draws one line per patient. Without it, ggplot would treat each timepoint as a separate group and have nothing to join.


colour = treatment
Colours each line by treatment group.


geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
Draws the lines, slightly thicker than the default.


geom_point(size = 2) +
Adds a point at each measurement.


scale_colour_manual(values = ...)
Chooses the colours yourself, rather than using ggplot’s defaults. Each group name is matched to a colour code (a hex code: # and six characters).


labs(x = NULL, ...)
Sets the axis and legend labels; NULL removes the x-axis title, which isn’t needed here.


theme_minimal()
A plainer background than ggplot’s default grey.





From long to wide
pivot_wider() goes the other way. You’ll need it occasionally, for example for a paired t-test in week 4, which wants the two measurements on each patient side by side:

bp_long |> pivot_wider(names_from = timepoint, values_from = sbp)

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  patient treatment Baseline `Week 12`
  <chr>   <chr>        <dbl>     <dbl>
1 P01     Drug           148       136
2 P02     Placebo        135       133
3 P03     Drug           160       145
4 P04     Placebo        142       141


Neither shape is “wrong”: wide is easier to read and type, long is what most analysis and plotting functions need. What matters is being able to move between them.

Step 8: Summaries by group
Once data is tidy, group_by() followed by summarise() gives a summary for every group. You’ll do much more of this in session 2; here is the basic pattern:

bp_long |>
  group_by(treatment, timepoint) |>
  summarise(
    n = sum(!is.na(sbp)),
    mean_sbp = mean(sbp, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

  (`?dplyr::dplyr_by`) instead.

2 Drug      Week 12       2     140.

4 Placebo   Week 12       2     137 









Code
What it does




group_by(treatment, timepoint)
Splits the data into groups: one for each combination of treatment and timepoint. Nothing visible happens yet.


summarise(
Calculates one row of summaries for each group.


n = sum(!is.na(sbp)),
Counts the values in each group that aren’t missing.


mean_sbp = mean(sbp, na.rm = TRUE)
The mean blood pressure in each group.


ungroup()
Removes the grouping from the result, so later steps treat it as one ordinary table.



The message about “grouped output” is information, not an error. When you group by two variables, summarise() removes the last grouping level but keeps the first, and it tells you so. ungroup() removes what’s left. It’s a good habit, because a table that is still grouped can give surprising results in later steps.

title: Guide to R 03: Tidy data and wrangling
text:
Putting it all together
In your own work, once each step has been checked, it’s good practice to collect the whole cleaning process into a single chunk that starts from the raw file. Anyone (including you, in six months’ time) can then see every decision in one place and re-run it from scratch:

patients_clean <- read_csv("data/Dataset.csv") |>
  clean_names() |>
  rename(wbc = wbc_count_10_9_l) |>
  mutate(
    # "High" can't be converted, so it becomes NA (see Step 3)
    crp_mg_l = as.numeric(crp_mg_l),
    sex = str_to_lower(sex),
    sex = case_when(
      sex %in% c("m", "male") ~ "Male",
      sex %in% c("f", "female") ~ "Female"
    ),
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c("Female", "Male")),
    covid_result = str_to_lower(covid_result),
    covid_result = str_remove_all(covid_result, '"'),
    covid_result = case_when(
      covid_result %in% c("positive", "pos") ~ "Positive",
      covid_result %in% c("negative", "neg") ~ "Negative"
    ),
    covid_result = factor(covid_result, levels = c("Negative", "Positive")),
    # "T" is ambiguous, so it is left to become NA (see Step 4)
    follow_up_required = case_when(
      follow_up_required %in% c("Yes", "Y") ~ "Yes",
      follow_up_required %in% c("No", "n") ~ "No"
    )
  )

section: Where R looks for files: the working directory
text:
Where R looks for files: the working directory
R reads files from, and saves files to, a particular folder known as the working directory. When you write read_csv("Dataset.csv"), R looks for Dataset.csv in the working directory and nowhere else. To find out what your working directory is, or to list the files in it, run:

getwd() # Tells you which folder is your working directory
list.files() # Lists all the files in the working directory

You may see code online that changes the working directory with setwd():

setwd("C:/Path/to/Working_Directory/Folder") # Avoid this in your own code

setwd() works, but the path inside it only exists on the computer it was written on. A script that uses it breaks as soon as you move it, share it with someone, or open it on a university PC. RStudio Projects solve this problem.

title: Guide to R 02: Projects, importing data and a first plot
text:
RStudio Projects
An RStudio Project is simply a folder with a small .Rproj file inside it. When you open a project, RStudio sets the working directory to the project folder for you. That means every path in your code can be written relative to the project folder, and the same code works on any computer the folder is copied to.

Creating a project

Go to File › New Project › New Directory › New Project.
Give the directory a name (for this module, R_module) and choose where to create it: somewhere you will find again and that is backed up, such as your university OneDrive.
Click Create Project. RStudio restarts inside the new project, and the project’s name appears at the top right of the window.

To come back to the project later, double-click the .Rproj file, or use File › Recent Projects.


Organising the project folder
For this module, keep your workbooks in the top level of the project folder and data in a subfolder called data:
R_module/
├── R_module.Rproj
├── week-01-session-1-workbook.qmd
├── week-01-session-2-workbook.qmd
└── data/
    └── Dataset.csv
With this layout, the path from the project folder to the data file is data/Dataset.csv. Code in a Quarto document runs from the folder the document is saved in, which here is also the project folder, so the same path works in your workbook and in the Console.


Managing files in the files pane
The Files pane shows the contents of the project folder, and you can use it like a file explorer:

Packages and the tidyverse
R on its own (“base R”) can do a great deal, but much of its power comes from packages: collections of functions that other people have written and shared. In this module we use the tidyverse, a family of packages designed to work together for importing, tidying, transforming and plotting data. It includes readr (importing), dplyr (choosing and changing rows and columns) and ggplot2 (plots).
Using a package takes two steps, and the difference between them causes a lot of confusion:








Step
Code
How often




Install the package: download it onto the computer
install.packages("tidyverse")
Once per computer (and again after updating R). Type it in the Console, not in a script or workbook.


Load the package: make its functions available in this session
library(tidyverse)
Every session. Put it at the top of every script and workbook.



On university computers the tidyverse may already be installed; check the Packages pane, or just try library(tidyverse) and see whether you get an error.

library(tidyverse)

✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2

text:
Organising data in Excel for importing into RStudio
Before analysing data in R, it is essential to structure it properly in Excel (or other spreadsheet software like Google Sheets). Poorly formatted data can cause errors when importing into R, so taking the time to organise it correctly will save time and effort later.

Basic rules for structuring data in Excel
To ensure a smooth import into R, follow these best practices when organising your dataset in Excel:

Use a clear table structure – Each row represents an observation, and each column represents a variable.
Include column headers – The first row should contain variable names (e.g., “Name”, “Age”, “Score”).
Avoid merging cells – Every cell should contain a single value without merging across rows or columns.
Do not leave blank rows or columns – Empty spaces can disrupt R’s ability to read data correctly.
Be consistent with data types – A column should contain only one type of data (e.g., numbers, text, or dates).
Avoid special characters or spaces in column names – Stick to letters, numbers, and underscores (e.g., Customer_ID instead of Customer ID!).



Example of a well-formatted dataset in Excel
A correctly structured dataset should look something like this:

Name
Age

Date_Joined

Why this works well:

Each column has a clear name.
No spaces or special characters in column titles.
All data types are consistent within each column (e.g., numbers in the “Age” column, text in “Name”, and dates in “Date_Joined”).
No merged cells or unnecessary formatting.



Saving the Excel file for R
Once the dataset is formatted correctly, save it in a format that R can easily read. The most common format for R is CSV (Comma-Separated Values).
Steps to save as CSV:

Click File > Save As.
Choose CSV (Comma delimited) (*.csv) as the file type.
Click Save.

CSV files are plain text, making them easier for R to read. Unlike .xlsx files, CSVs do not contain extra formatting, reducing potential import issues. CSV files are also compatible with most data analysis tools.

title: Guide to R 02: Projects, importing data and a first plot
text:
Importing a CSV file
The examples below use the file Dataset.csv, a small, deliberately messy COVID-related dataset. Opened as plain text, this is what it contains:


Patient_ID,Age,Sex,CRP_mg.L,WBC_Count_10^9.L,COVID_Result,FollowUp_Required
P001,45,M,12.5,8.4,Positive,Yes
P002,38,F,8.1,7.2,positive,Y
P003,52,male,NA,6.9,NEG,No
P004,29,Female,5.3,NA,"""negative""",n
P005,NA,M,High,10.2,Pos,T


We import it with read_csv() from the readr package, giving the path from the project folder to the file, and store the result in an object called patients:

patients <- read_csv("data/Dataset.csv")

Rows: 5 Columns: 7
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (5): Patient_ID, Sex, CRP_mg.L, COVID_Result, FollowUp_Required
dbl (2): Age, WBC_Count_10^9.L

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.


Read this message. It tells you how many rows and columns were imported and what type of data R decided each column holds: chr (character, i.e. text) or dbl (double, i.e. a number). Already there is a warning sign. CRP_mg.L should hold numbers, but R has read it as text. We’ll see why, and fix it, below.
If you need a file that isn’t in your project, you can give a full path instead. On Windows, copy the path from File Explorer and change every \ to /, because R treats \ as a special character. But a path like this only works on your own computer, which is why we keep data inside the project.

patients <- read_csv("C:/Users/yourname/Documents/Dataset.csv")







Noteread_csv() and read.csv()



In other people’s code you will often see read.csv(), with a full stop. That is base R’s version. It works, but read_csv() is faster, tells you what type it has given each column, keeps column names exactly as they are in the file, and creates a tibble (see below). Use read_csv() in this module.

title: Guide to R 02: Projects, importing data and a first plot
text:
Checking what you have imported
After importing a dataset, the first thing to do is check its structure, to understand the types of variables and detect any issues. Three functions do most of the work:

glimpse(patients) # One line per column: its type and its first few values

Rows: 5
Columns: 7
$ Patient_ID         <chr> "P001", "P002", "P003", "P004", "P005"
$ Age                <dbl> 45, 38, 52, 29, NA
$ Sex                <chr> "M", "F", "male", "Female", "M"
$ CRP_mg.L           <chr> "12.5", "8.1", NA, "5.3", "High"
$ `WBC_Count_10^9.L` <dbl> 8.4, 7.2, 6.9, NA, 10.2
$ COVID_Result       <chr> "Positive", "positive", "NEG", "\"negative\"", "Pos"
$ FollowUp_Required  <chr> "Yes", "Y", "No", "n", "T"



head(patients) # The first few rows, as a table

# A tibble: 5 × 7
  Patient_ID   Age Sex    CRP_mg.L `WBC_Count_10^9.L` COVID_Result  
  <chr>      <dbl> <chr>  <chr>                 <dbl> <chr>         
1 P001          45 M      12.5                    8.4 "Positive"    
2 P002          38 F      8.1                     7.2 "positive"    
3 P003          52 male   <NA>                    6.9 "NEG"         
4 P004          29 Female 5.3                    NA   "\"negative\""
5 P005          NA M      High                   10.2 "Pos"         
# ℹ 1 more variable: FollowUp_Required <chr>



summary(patients) # Summary statistics for each column

     Patient_ID      Age               Sex         CRP_mg.L WBC_Count_10^9.L
 Length   :5    Min.   :29.00   Length   :5   Length   :5   Min.   : 6.900  
 N.unique :5    1st Qu.:35.75   N.unique :4   N.unique :4   1st Qu.: 7.125  
 N.blank  :0    Median :41.50   N.blank  :0   N.blank  :0   Median : 7.800  
 Min.nchar:4    Mean   :41.00   Min.nchar:1   Min.nchar:3   Mean   : 8.175  
 Max.nchar:4    3rd Qu.:46.75   Max.nchar:6   Max.nchar:4   3rd Qu.: 8.850  
                Max.   :52.00                 NAs      :1   Max.   :10.200  
                NAs    :1                                   NAs    :1       
    COVID_Result FollowUp_Required
 Length   : 5    Length   :5      
 N.unique : 5    N.unique :5      
 N.blank  : 0    N.blank  :0      
 Min.nchar: 3    Min.nchar:1      
 Max.nchar:10    Max.nchar:3      
                                  
                                  


When beginning any data analysis in R, functions like glimpse(), head() and summary() serve as foundational quality checks. They are not just for familiarising yourself with the dataset, but to systematically verify that the data is structured correctly, contains appropriate variable types, and has no obvious flaws that would compromise downstream analysis.
head() gives a quick preview of the first rows of the dataset. This is an immediate way to confirm that the data has been imported correctly: column names should match expectations, each row should represent an individual observation, and the values should appear sensible at a glance. If there are shifted headers or corrupted entries, this will become obvious immediately.
glimpse() provides more technical insight into the internal structure of the dataset. Specifically, it reveals the data type of each variable, as well as the number of observations and columns. (Base R’s str() does the same job, and you will see it in older code.) This is important because many statistical procedures in R require variables to be of specific types. For example, logistic regression expects the outcome variable to be a factor rather than a character string, and plotting functions behave differently depending on whether a variable is treated as categorical or continuous. In the output above, CRP_mg.L is <chr> because one entry is the word “High”, and a single piece of text is enough to make R read the whole column as text.
summary() gives a statistical overview of each variable. For numeric variables, it returns the minimum, maximum, mean, median, and quartiles, allowing you to spot skewed distributions, extreme values, or potentially erroneous data points (e.g., a blood pressure reading of 400 mmHg). The presence of missing values (NA's) is also evident in this output. Notice that for CRP_mg.L it can only report that the column is character: there are no numbers to summarise.
Together, these three commands act as a diagnostic triad. Skipping these checks risks proceeding with poorly structured or corrupted data, potentially leading to flawed or invalid results. The start-up and troubleshooting guide lists the full set of checks to run at the start of every analysis.

Column names that break R’s naming rules
One column is called WBC_Count_10^9.L. The ^ isn’t allowed in an R name, so whenever you refer to this column you must wrap its name in backticks (`), which you can see glimpse() doing above. It is usually easier to rename it, which you’ll do with rename() once you’ve met the pipe below.

title: Guide to R 02: Projects, importing data and a first plot
text:
Data frames and tibbles
A data frame is R’s version of a table: each column is a vector (so everything in a column has the same type), and each row is one observation. The tidyverse uses a modern version of the data frame called a tibble, which prints more neatly and is a little stricter about mistakes. You can treat the two words as meaning the same thing.
You can also build a tibble yourself, column by column:

students <- tibble(
  Name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"), # First column (character vector)
  Age = c(25, 24, 23), # Second column (numeric vector)
  Score = c(90, 85, 88) # Third column (numeric vector)
)
students

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  Name      Age Score
  <chr>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 Alice      25    90
2 Bob        24    85
3 Charlie    23    88









Code
Explanation




students <-
Creates a new object called students to store the tibble.


tibble(...)
This function creates a tibble, a table-like structure where each column can be a different type.


Name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie")
The first column. It’s a character vector with the names of three students.


Age = c(25, 24, 23)
The second column. It’s a numeric vector representing the students’ ages.


Score = c(90, 85, 88)
The third column. Another numeric vector, this time showing scores or marks for each student.



In other people’s code you’ll also see a single column pulled out with $, which gives you that column as a vector:

students$Score

[1] 90 85 88

title: Guide to R 02: Projects, importing data and a first plot
text:
The pipe, |>
Most tidyverse code is written as a series of steps joined by the pipe, |>. The pipe takes whatever is on its left and passes it to the function on its right as the first argument. You can read it as “and then”.

students |> filter(Score > 86)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  Name      Age Score
  <chr>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 Alice      25    90
2 Charlie    23    88


This reads: “take students, and then keep the rows where Score is greater than 86”. It does exactly the same as filter(students, Score > 86), but once you chain several steps together, the piped version is much easier to read from top to bottom. The keyboard shortcut is Ctrl + Shift + M (Cmd + Shift + M on a Mac).






Tip|> and %>%



In older code and online examples you’ll see %>% instead of |>. It comes from the magrittr package and does almost exactly the same job. If Ctrl + Shift + M gives you %>%, tick Use native pipe operator in Tools › Global Options › Code.

title: Guide to R 02: Projects, importing data and a first plot
section: Choosing rows and columns with dplyr
text:
Choosing rows and columns with dplyr
Five dplyr functions cover most of what you need to do with a table. Each takes a tibble and gives back a new tibble, so they can be chained with the pipe.








Function
What it does
Example




select()
Keeps (or drops) columns
select(Name, Score)


filter()
Keeps rows that meet a condition
filter(Age < 25)


arrange()
Sorts rows
arrange(desc(Score))


mutate()
Creates a new column, or changes an existing one
mutate(Age_months = Age * 12)


summarise()
Reduces many rows to a single summary row
summarise(mean_score = mean(Score))




students |> select(Name, Score)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  Name    Score
  <chr>   <dbl>
1 Alice      90
2 Bob        85
3 Charlie    88

students |> arrange(desc(Score))

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  Name      Age Score
  <chr>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 Alice      25    90
2 Charlie    23    88
3 Bob        24    85

students |> mutate(Age_months = Age * 12)

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  Name      Age Score Age_months
  <chr>   <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>
1 Alice      25    90        300
2 Bob        24    85        288
3 Charlie    23    88        276

students |> summarise(mean_score = mean(Score))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  mean_score
       <dbl>
1       87.7


Conditions inside filter() use the same comparison operators you met with vectors:

== equal to (two equals signs: a single = is for naming arguments);
!= not equal to;
>, >=, <, <= greater than, at least, less than, at most;
%in% matches any value in a list, e.g. Name %in% c("Alice", "Bob");
& and, | or, ! not, for combining conditions; and
is.na() is missing.

None of these functions changes the original tibble. To keep the result, assign it to a name:

high_scores <- students |> filter(Score > 86)

And here is the renaming promised above, using the patients data:

patients <- patients |> rename(WBC = `WBC_Count_10^9.L`)
names(patients)

[1] "Patient_ID"        "Age"               "Sex"              
[4] "CRP_mg.L"          "WBC"               "COVID_Result"     
[7] "FollowUp_Required"

title: Guide to R 02: Projects, importing data and a first plot
section: When numbers are stored as text
text:
When numbers are stored as text
Here is why checking types matters. Suppose we want the patients whose CRP is above 10 mg/L:

patients |> filter(CRP_mg.L > 10)

# A tibble: 4 × 7
  Patient_ID   Age Sex    CRP_mg.L   WBC COVID_Result   FollowUp_Required
  <chr>      <dbl> <chr>  <chr>    <dbl> <chr>          <chr>            
1 P001          45 M      12.5       8.4 "Positive"     Yes              
2 P002          38 F      8.1        7.2 "positive"     Y                
3 P004          29 Female 5.3       NA   "\"negative\"" n                
4 P005          NA M      High      10.2 "Pos"          T                


R returns four patients, including CRP values of 8.1 and 5.3, and the word “High”. It hasn’t given an error or a warning, just a wrong answer. Because CRP_mg.L is text, R compares it as text, alphabetically and character by character: “8.1” comes after “10” because “8” comes after “1”, so it counts as “greater”.
The fix is to convert the column to numbers with mutate() and as.numeric():

patients <- patients |> mutate(CRP_mg.L = as.numeric(CRP_mg.L))

Warning: There was 1 warning in `mutate()`.
ℹ In argument: `CRP_mg.L = as.numeric(CRP_mg.L)`.
Caused by warning:
! NAs introduced by coercion

patients |> filter(CRP_mg.L > 10)

# A tibble: 1 × 7
  Patient_ID   Age Sex   CRP_mg.L   WBC COVID_Result FollowUp_Required
  <chr>      <dbl> <chr>    <dbl> <dbl> <chr>        <chr>            
1 P001          45 M         12.5   8.4 Positive     Yes              


R warns that some values became NA: “High” can’t be turned into a number. That warning is useful. Whether “High” should become a missing value, or something else, is a decision about your data, and one you should record in your write-up. Next week you’ll meet more of these cleaning decisions.

title: Guide to R 02: Projects, importing data and a first plot
text:
A first plot with ggplot2
ggplot2 builds a plot in layers, from three ingredients:

the data, a tibble or data frame;
the aesthetic mappings, aes(), which say which columns go on which axis (and, later, which control colour, fill and so on); and
one or more geoms, the shapes that represent the data: points, boxes, bars, lines.

Layers are added with +.
To have enough data for an interesting plot, we’ll use ToothGrowth, a dataset that comes with R. It records the length of odontoblasts (the cells responsible for tooth growth) in 60 guinea pigs, each of which received one of three doses of vitamin C (0.5, 1 or 2 mg/day) by one of two methods: orange juice (OJ) or ascorbic acid (VC).

glimpse(ToothGrowth)

Rows: 60
Columns: 3
$ len  <dbl> 4.2, 11.5, 7.3, 5.8, 6.4, 10.0, 11.2, 11.2, 5.2, 7.0, 16.5, 16.5,…
$ supp <fct> VC, VC, VC, VC, VC, VC, VC, VC, VC, VC, VC, VC, VC, VC, VC, VC, V…
$ dose <dbl> 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, …



ggplot(ToothGrowth, aes(x = factor(dose), y = len)) +
  geom_boxplot()








factor(dose) tells ggplot to treat the three doses as separate groups rather than as points on a number line. Adding a second geom shows the individual animals on top of the boxes:

ggplot(ToothGrowth, aes(x = factor(dose), y = len)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1)








Mapping a third column to fill splits each dose by supplement type, and labs() gives the plot proper labels:

ggplot(ToothGrowth, aes(x = factor(dose), y = len, fill = supp)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    x = "Vitamin C dose (mg/day)",
    y = "Odontoblast length",
    fill = "Supplement"
  )








Tooth growth increases with dose, and at the two lower doses orange juice seems to produce longer odontoblasts than ascorbic acid. Whether those differences are bigger than chance would produce is a question for week 4, when you meet ANOVA.






Warning+ not |>



The layers of a ggplot are joined with +, not with the pipe. Using |> between ggplot() and geom_boxplot() is one of the most common beginner errors, and ggplot’s error message will usually suggest the fix.

title: Guide to R 02: Projects, importing data and a first plot
text:
Saving your work
To save a plot, run ggsave() straight after making it. To save a tibble as a CSV file, use write_csv(). In both cases the path is relative to the project folder; create a figures folder in the Files pane first if you use the one below.

ggsave("figures/toothgrowth.png", width = 6, height = 4) # Saves the last plot you made
write_csv(patients, "data/patients_checked.csv") # row names are never added, unlike write.csv()

title: Guide to R 00: Start-up and troubleshooting
text:
This guide provides a structured routine to follow at the beginning of every data analysis session, taking you from opening R through to having a dataset that is clean, consistent, and ready for statistical testing. In practice, most analytical problems don’t arise from the statistical methods themselves but from issues such as files being loaded from the wrong location, variables being stored in the wrong format, inconsistent category labels, hidden missing values, or parts of the environment not being properly initialised. Working through the same sequence of checks each time helps you detect these problems early, reduces time spent trying to diagnose errors later, and supports a reproducible workflow in which your results can be repeated and justified.
There is also a troubleshooting guide at the end. The start-up checks help you prevent common problems before they occur, while the troubleshooting guide helps you interpret error messages and identify what has gone wrong when something doesn’t run as expected. Together they form a complete workflow: first you confirm that your data and environment are correct, and then, if an error still occurs, you have a clear process for diagnosing and fixing it. By the end of these steps you should be confident that you are analysing the correct dataset, that your variables are in the appropriate format for your chosen method, and that you have the information required to answer your research question in a transparent and reproducible way.
The examples use the tidyverse and assume your data is in an object called data, with made-up column names (sex, age, group and so on). Replace them with your own.

Cleaning and standardising variables








What to do
Example R code
What you are fixing




Standardise text to lower case
data <- data |> mutate(sex = str_to_lower(sex))
Makes F, f, Female consistent


Remove extra spaces
data <- data |> mutate(sex = str_trim(sex))
Fixes hidden spaces


Recode several labels into one category each
data <- data |> mutate(sex = case_when(sex %in% c("f", "female") ~ "female", sex %in% c("m", "male") ~ "male", .default = sex))
Combines duplicate categories, leaving anything unexpected unchanged so you can spot it


Check the result
count(data, sex)
Confirms categories are correct


Convert to factor
data <- data |> mutate(sex = factor(sex))
Makes variable usable in analysis


Convert numbers stored as text

Numbers stored as text (R warns if any value can’t be converted)


Convert grouping variables to factors
data <- data |> mutate(group = factor(group))
Correct statistical handling


Give numeric group codes labels
data <- data |> mutate(group = factor(group, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("control", "treatment")))
Makes output interpretable

title: Guide to R 00: Start-up and troubleshooting
text:
Troubleshooting







Issue / error message
Try / check this




Object not found
This almost always means the object hasn’t been created in the current session or its name doesn’t exactly match. R is case sensitive, so data, Data and DATA are different. Run the line where the object is created, check the spelling, and use ls() to see what objects actually exist in the environment.


Could not find function (e.g. "read_csv" or "ggplot")
The package that contains the function hasn’t been loaded in this session. Run library(tidyverse), and make sure it is at the top of your script or workbook.


There is no package called…
The package isn’t installed on this computer. Install it once, in the Console: install.packages("tidyverse").


I ran the script but nothing happened
R only executes the lines you send to the console. Highlight the code and press Run, or place the cursor on the line and use the run shortcut (Ctrl + Enter). Just opening a script does not execute it.


The function worked yesterday but not today
The session has been restarted and required packages have not been loaded. Re-run the library() calls at the top of the script, for example library(tidyverse). In a reproducible script, package loading should always be included at the beginning.


Cannot find the file / does not exist in current working directory
R looks for files relative to the working directory. Check that you have opened your project (its name shows at the top right of RStudio), then confirm the file is where your code says it is with list.files() or list.files("data"). The fix is usually to move the file into the project, or correct the path in your code, rather than calling setwd().


The file is in my folder but R still cannot see it
Check the exact file name and extension. Windows may hide extensions, so what looks like data might actually be data.csv.csv. Use list.files() to see the true name and match it exactly in the code.


Unexpected symbol or unexpected input
This usually means a missing quote, bracket, or comma on the previous line. R often flags the error where it notices the problem, not where it started. Check the line above for unclosed quotes (" " or ' '), brackets ( ) or braces { }.


My column name does not work in the code
Column names must match exactly. Use names(data) to inspect them. If they contain spaces or special characters, either wrap them in backticks (`Blood Pressure`) or rename them with rename() or janitor::clean_names().


filter() error mentioning a “named input”
You have used = where you meant ==, e.g. filter(dose = 2). Use two equals signs to test whether values are equal.


ggplot error suggesting you used |> or %>% instead of +
The layers of a ggplot are joined with +, not with the pipe.


I created the object but it has disappeared
You may have restarted the session, cleared the environment, or run only part of the script. In a good workflow the script should run from top to bottom without relying on previously created objects.


I ran a dplyr step but the data hasn’t changed
filter(), mutate() and friends return a new tibble; they don’t change the original. To keep the result, assign it: data <- data |> mutate(...).


The output looks wrong after I imported the data
Check the structure with glimpse(data), and re-read read_csv()’s message. The most common issue is a numeric variable being read as character because of non-numeric entries such as text (“High”, “<5”) or missing-value codes.


Numbers are being treated as text
This happens when a column contains non-numeric characters. Use as.numeric() or parse_number() once you have decided what to do with the non-numeric entries, or tell read_csv() which codes mean “missing” with its na = argument, e.g. read_csv("data/data.csv", na = c("", "NA", "999")).


Package is installed but the function is not found
Installing a package is not the same as loading it. You still need library(package_name) in the script.


There is a red plus sign in the console and R will not run
R is waiting for you to finish the command. This likely means a bracket or quote hasn’t been closed. Press Esc to break out, then fix the incomplete line.


My script works line by line but not when I run it all at once
This indicates the script depends on objects created interactively or in the wrong order. Reorganise the script so that data import, cleaning, and analysis occur in a logical sequence and the environment starts empty.


I saved the script but the changes are not reflected
Saving the script does not re-run it. The updated code must be executed again.


My Quarto document won’t render, but every chunk ran fine interactively
Rendering starts R from scratch and runs the document from top to bottom. Something the document needs was only ever created in the Console (often a library() call). Restart R, then use Run All to find the first chunk that fails.

title: Guide to R 01: R and RStudio basics
text:
What is R?
R is a powerful programming language specifically designed for statistical computing and data analysis. It is widely used in academia, research, and industry for handling data, performing statistical tests, and creating visualisations. Unlike general-purpose programming languages such as Python or Java, R was built with data in mind, making it particularly well-suited for statistical modelling, machine learning, and data manipulation.
However, working with R directly can feel intimidating at first, as it primarily runs through a command-line interface. This is where RStudio comes in.
RStudio is an integrated development environment (IDE) that makes working with R much more accessible and user-friendly. It provides a structured interface where users can write, run, and debug R code more efficiently. RStudio includes helpful features such as:

A script editor – allowing users to write and save R code in files for reuse.
A console – where commands are executed immediately.
An environment pane – displaying stored variables and datasets.
A plots and files pane – for viewing visualisations, managing files, and installing packages.

Together, R and RStudio form a powerful toolkit for data analysis. R handles the computation, while RStudio provides an organised workspace to interact with R more effectively. Throughout this guide, you will learn how to use both tools to perform data analysis, create visualisations, and explore datasets in an intuitive and structured manner.

section: Getting started with RStudio: your first look
text:
Getting started with RStudio: your first look
When you open RStudio for the first time, you will see a workspace divided into multiple panes. While this layout may seem overwhelming at first, each section serves a specific purpose. Let’s go through what you should do to get started.

Familiarising yourself with the interface
RStudio is divided into four main panes:

The Script Editor (top-left pane, may be empty at first) – This is where you write and save R scripts (files ending in .R).
The Environment and History Pane (top-right) – Shows stored variables, datasets, and a history of past commands.
The Console (bottom-left pane) – This is where you can type R commands and see immediate results.
The Files, Plots, Packages, and Help Pane (bottom-right) – Used for managing files, viewing plots, installing packages, and accessing documentation.



Script editor
The Script Editor (also called the Source panel) in RStudio is where you write, edit, and save R scripts (.R files), R Markdown (.Rmd) documents and Quarto (.qmd) documents such as your workbook. It is designed for writing reusable code, rather than running commands directly in the Console.


Key features of the script editor

Code writing & editing: type and edit R scripts.
Code execution: run selected lines or entire scripts.
Syntax highlighting: different colours for functions, variables, and comments.
Auto-completion: suggests function names and arguments.
Code folding: collapse or expand sections of long scripts.
Multiple tabs: open multiple scripts at the same time.



Explanation of buttons & tools in the script editor
In the screenshot, several buttons and tools appear at the top of the Script Editor.

Toolbar buttons






Button
Function




Save
Saves the current script to a .R file.


Open File
Opens an existing R script.


New Script
Creates a new R script.


Source on Save
Runs the script automatically when saved.


Run
Runs selected code or the current line.


Source
Runs the whole script in the Console (useful for functions).





Running code from the script editor
There are three main ways to execute code from the Script Editor:









Method
Shortcut (Windows/Linux)
Shortcut (Mac)
Action




Run selected line
Ctrl + Enter
Cmd + Enter
Runs the current line where the cursor is placed.


Run multiple lines
Select lines + Ctrl + Enter
Select lines + Cmd + Enter
Runs the selected block of code.


Run entire script
Ctrl + Shift + S
Cmd + Shift + S
Runs (sources) the full script from top to bottom.





Managing multiple scripts in tabs
You can open multiple scripts at once in different tabs: just click the “+” (New Script) button to start a new script. You can switch between scripts using the tab navigation at the top.


Saving your script
To save your work:

Click File > Save As…
Choose a filename (e.g., my_script.R).
Click Save.

Always save your scripts regularly to avoid losing progress.


Why use the script editor instead of the console?








Feature
Script Editor (.R file)
Console




Reusable code
Saves code for future use
Code disappears after execution


Runs multiple lines
Can run an entire script
Runs only one command at a time


Error debugging
Easier to edit and fix errors
Need to retype fixed code


Organisation
Can document workflow
Hard to keep track of past commands





Summary of key features








Feature
Shortcut / Button
Purpose




Run line of code
Ctrl + Enter
Runs the current line.


Run entire script
Ctrl + Shift + S
Runs the full script.


Save script
Ctrl + S
Saves your work.


Syntax highlighting
Automatic
Helps read code easily.


Multiple tabs
+ button
Open multiple scripts.






Environment pane
The Environment Pane is where all objects (datasets, variables, functions, and models) created during an R session are displayed. This pane helps users manage, inspect, and modify objects in the R workspace.


Key features of the environment pane







Feature
Function




Displays all active objects
Shows datasets, variables, lists, functions, and models currently loaded in R.


Organises objects by type
Groups objects as data frames, vectors, matrices, lists, and functions.


Allows object inspection
Click on an object to open and view its contents in a spreadsheet-like format.


Facilitates dataset import
Includes an Import Dataset button for loading files (CSV, Excel, SPSS, etc.).


Memory usage display
Shows the amount of memory currently used in the R session.





Components of the environment pane

Import Dataset button
Located at the top-left, this quickly imports datasets from different file formats. To import a dataset manually:

Click “Import Dataset”.
Choose a file format:

Text file (.csv, .txt)
Excel file (.xls, .xlsx)
SPSS, Stata, or SAS file

Use the preview window to check the data before importing.
Click “Import” – the dataset will appear in the Environment Pane.

Alternatively, use code in the Console or through the Script Editor to import a dataset:

data <- read_csv("file.csv") # Imports the dataset "file" and gives it the name "data"
View(data) # Opens the dataset in a new tab

You’ll import data properly in session 2, where the Guide to R 02 explains read_csv().


Global environment dropdown
The Global Environment menu shows all currently loaded objects. If an object exists, you can expand/collapse it to see details. You can click the dropdown arrow to clear the environment or filter objects.




Memory usage indicator
The memory indicator tracks memory usage for efficient performance. If RStudio is slow, you might want to clear large objects to free memory. To check how much memory a particular object is using, run:

format(object.size(data), units = "auto") # Shows the size of the object called data



Object list and search bar
You can see the list of items loaded in the Environment pane. You can use the search bar (top-right) to find specific objects in large environments.



Managing objects in the environment







Action
Method




Remove a single object
rm(object_name)


Remove all objects
rm(list = ls())


View dataset in table format
View(data)


Check object structure
str(object_name)


Check variable names in a dataset
names(data)






Console pane
The Console Pane is where R executes commands and displays output. It is the interactive interface for running R code in real time.


Key features of the console pane







Feature
Function




Execute commands
Type commands and press Enter to run them immediately.


View outputs
Displays results of calculations, summaries, and errors.


Debugging & errors
Shows error messages if commands fail.


Session information
Displays the R version, workspace path, and startup messages.





Interactive help and demos
R provides built-in help:







Command
Function




help()
Opens general help.


help("mean")
Shows help for a specific function (mean).


help.start()
Opens an HTML help browser.


demo()
Lists available demos.



If you want to get help for a specific function, you can use the code:

help("lm") # Shows documentation for linear models (lm)



Running commands in the console
The > symbol at the bottom is the command prompt, where you can type R code. Press Enter after each command to execute it.

x <- 10 # Assigns the value of 10 to x
y <- x * 2 # Performs the calculation x * 2 (10 x 2) and assigns it the name y
print(y) # Outputs the value for y to the console

[1] 20




Exiting R from the console
To exit R, type:

q()

You will be asked whether to save your workspace before quitting.






TipDon’t save your workspace



Choose Don’t Save. Saving the workspace stores every object in a hidden .RData file and quietly reloads it next time, so your analysis can appear to work when it actually depends on objects your script no longer creates. Turn this off permanently in Tools › Global Options › General: untick Restore .RData into workspace at startup and set Save workspace to .RData on exit to Never. Your scripts and workbooks are the record of your work; the workspace isn’t.




Clearing the console
If the Console is cluttered, you can clear it:







Method
Shortcut




Windows/Linux
Ctrl + L


Mac
Cmd + L



Alternatively, run the code:

cat("\014") # Clears the console




Summary of console commands







Command
Purpose




R.version.string
Check R version.


license()
View licence details.


help("function")
Open function help.


q()
Quit R.


Ctrl + L
Clear the Console.





Files pane
The Files Pane allows you to navigate, manage, and organise files within your R project directory. It functions like a file explorer, providing access to scripts, datasets, images, and other resources used in your analysis.


Key features of the files pane







Feature
Function




File navigation
Browse project directories and access files.


Create & edit files
Create new R scripts, text files, and folders.


Rename & delete
Modify or remove files directly from RStudio.


Open R projects (.Rproj)
Manage project workspaces.


History & logs (.Rhistory)
View previously executed commands.



R reads files from, and saves files to, a particular folder called the working directory. In session 2 you’ll learn how that works, and how RStudio Projects take care of it for you; the Guide to R 02 covers both.

title: Guide to R 01: R and RStudio basics
text:
Commenting in R
In R, you can write comments in your code using the # symbol. Anything written after a # on a line is ignored by R when the code is run. Comments are used to explain what your code does or leave notes for yourself or others.

Why use comments?







Purpose
Explanation




Explain your code
Comments make it easier to understand what each part of your code is doing.


Improve readability
Future-you (or someone else) will thank you when revisiting the code later.


Test or debug code
You can “turn off” parts of your code without deleting them.


Make teaching notes
Helpful for sharing code with students or collaborators.





Examples of good commenting

data <- read.csv("my_data.csv") # Load the dataset from a CSV file
average_age <- mean(data$Age) # Get the mean of the Age column
hist(data$BMI, main = "Distribution of BMI") # Plot a histogram of BMI values



What not to do
Avoid over-commenting things that are obvious:

# Set x to 10
x <- 10 # This is clear already – comment may be unnecessary

And avoid writing unclear or inconsistent comments:

x <- 10 # oh this is something to do with age maybe?



Commenting blocks of code
R doesn’t support multi-line block comments like some other languages, but you can still comment multiple lines manually. (In RStudio, select the lines and press Ctrl + Shift + C to comment or uncomment them all at once.)

# This block of code does a t-test
# between Group A and Group B
# to check for significant differences
t.test(groupA, groupB)



Summary







Do
Don’t




Use comments to explain why things are done
Comment every single obvious line


Keep comments clear and relevant
Let comments get out of date


Use comments to organise long scripts
Use vague or cryptic notes


Comment out code while testing
Delete useful lines too quickly
