title: Guide to R 01: R and RStudio basics
text:
Variables, functions and vectors
Each line of R code contains different elements, including functions, arguments, operators, variables, and values. Understanding these elements will help you read and write R code with confidence.

Variables in R
A variable in R is a named storage location that holds a value, which can be reused and manipulated in future calculations. By assigning a value to a variable, we tell R to remember that value under a specific name so we can reference it later in our code.







Advantage
Explanation




Avoids repetition
Instead of retyping values, store them in variables for easy reuse.


Makes code readable
Variables with meaningful names clarify what data represents.


Allows dynamic changes
Modify the variable’s value once, and all dependent calculations update automatically.


Supports complex calculations
Break down large problems by storing intermediate results in variables.



If we don’t use variables, we can make life harder for ourselves. Here, 5 is hardcoded multiple times, making it repetitive and harder to modify.

print(5 * 10)

[1] 50

print(5 * 20)

[1] 100

print(5 * 30)

[1] 150


If we instead store 5 in a variable and later need to change the multiplier to another value, we only change x once, and all calculations we run from that point on will update accordingly.

x <- 5 # Assign value 5 to variable x
print(x * 10)

[1] 50

print(x * 20)

[1] 100

print(x * 30)

[1] 150



Assigning values to variables
In R, variables are assigned using <-

name <- "Alice" # Assigns the text 'Alice' to the variable 'name'
age <- 30 # Assigns the number 30 to the variable 'age'
height <- 1.75 # Assigns the decimal number 1.75 to the variable 'height'



Accessing and using variables
Once a variable is assigned, it can be used in further operations.

age <- 30 # Assigns the number 30 to the variable 'age'
print(age) # Outputs 30 to the screen

[1] 30

# Use the variable in calculations
next_year <- age + 1 # Assigns the value age + 1 to the variable 'next_year'
print(next_year) # Outputs the result of the calculation age + 1, here 30 + 1

[1] 31


We don’t need to retype 30 – R remembers it as age.


Updating variables
Variables in R can be reassigned new values, replacing the old value with the new one.

age <- 30 # Initial value
age <- 31 # Update value
print(age) # Outputs new value which is 31

[1] 31




Naming variables: rules & best practices
You need to follow certain rules when naming your variables:

Names must start with a letter (e.g., age, Height_kg).
Cannot contain spaces (use _ or . instead, e.g., max_speed or max.speed).
Case-sensitive (Height and height are different variables).
Cannot use reserved R keywords (e.g., if, else, TRUE, FALSE).

Best practices for naming variables:








Bad variable name
Why?
Better name




x
Too vague
patient_age


A.B
Confusing dot usage
blood_pressure


123abc
Starts with a number
abc123


temperature value
Contains spaces
temperature_value





Checking data type of a variable
Variables in R store different types of data (e.g. text or numbers). You can check a variable’s data type using class(). Understanding data types is important because different functions work with specific types.

x <- "Hello" # Assigns 'Hello' to the variable x
class(x) # Outputs that it's a character type

[1] "character"

y <- 25 # Assigns the value 25 to the variable y
class(y) # Outputs that it's a numeric type

[1] "numeric"

z <- TRUE # Assigns the logical value TRUE to the variable z
class(z) # Outputs that it's a logical type

[1] "logical"




Deleting variables
To remove a variable you are no longer using, or to free up memory when working with large datasets, use rm(). Once a variable has been removed, asking for it produces an error:

rm(age) # Deletes the variable 'age'
print(age) # Error: object 'age' not found

Error:
! object 'age' not found





Summary







Concept
Explanation




What is a variable?
A storage location that holds a value.


How to assign a variable?
Use <-, e.g., x <- 10.


Why use variables?
Avoids repetition, makes code readable, allows updates.


Naming rules
Start with a letter, no spaces, case-sensitive.


Check data type
Use class(variable_name).


Remove a variable
Use rm(variable_name).





Using functions
A function is a named piece of code that does a particular job. You have already used several: print(), class() and rm(). To use (or “call”) a function, you write its name followed by round brackets, and put the inputs it needs, called arguments, inside the brackets, separated by commas.

sqrt(81) # One argument: the number to take the square root of

[1] 9

round(3.14159) # Rounds to a whole number by default

[1] 3

round(3.14159, digits = 2) # A second argument changes how it behaves

[1] 3.14



Naming arguments
Arguments can be given by position or by name. round(3.14159, 2) and round(3.14159, digits = 2) do the same thing, but the second is easier to read, so it’s good practice to name every argument after the first.


Default values
Many arguments have a default: a value the function uses unless you say otherwise. round() uses digits = 0 unless you give it something else, which is why round(3.14159) gives 3. The default you’ll meet most often this week belongs to mean(): its na.rm argument is FALSE unless you change it, so a single missing value makes the whole result NA (see Watch out for missing values, below).


Finding out what a function does
Every function has a help page. Run help("round") or ?round in the Console and it opens in the Help pane. The Usage section shows the arguments and their defaults, the Arguments section explains each one, and the Examples at the bottom are code you can copy and run. Reading help pages is a skill worth building early: you’ll use it for every new function in this module.

?round









Term
Meaning
Example




Function
A named piece of code that does a job
round()


Argument
An input to a function
digits = 2


Default
The value an argument takes if you don’t give one
digits = 0 in round()


Help page
The documentation for a function
?round









NoteWriting your own functions



You can also write functions of your own. You won’t need to for now: everything in this module uses functions that already exist in R or in its packages.

title: Guide to R 01: R and RStudio basics
text:
Vectors: storing many values together
R has several ways of organising data, called data structures. Choosing the right one matters, because it determines which functions and operations you can use. In this session you’ll meet the most basic, the vector. In session 2 you’ll meet the data frame (in the tidyverse, a tibble), which is how R stores a table of data, and which is built out of vectors.

Vectors (1D data)
A vector in R is the most basic data structure, used to store a sequence of values of the same type. Vectors allow you to perform efficient mathematical operations, apply functions to multiple elements at once, and store data in a structured format.

Why use vectors in R?
Vectors are essential in R because they enable fast and efficient data manipulation.







Advantage
Explanation




Stores multiple values
Holds sequences of numbers, text, or logical values.


Efficient operations
Apply functions to all elements at once.


Easy indexing
Quickly extract or modify values.


Foundation of other data structures
Data frames and matrices are built using vectors.





Creating a vector
Vectors are created using the concatenate function, c(), which combines multiple values into a single object. Vectors can hold different types of data, but each vector can only store one type at a time. If you want to check what type of vector you have, you can use the class() command, the same as we did for the variable type.








Vector type
Example
Description




Numeric
c(10, 20, 30)
Stores numbers (integers or decimals).


Character
c("A", "B", "C")
Stores text values.


Logical
c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
Stores TRUE/FALSE values.




ages <- c(25, 30, 35, 40) # Groups the numbers 25, 30, 35, 40 into a vector and assigns it to the variable 'ages'
names <- c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie") # Groups the words Alice, Bob and Charlie into a vector and assigns it to the variable 'names'
responses <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE) # Groups the logical values TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE into a vector and assigns it to the variable 'responses'



Accessing vector elements
You can retrieve specific values using indexing ([ ]). Please note that R uses 1-based indexing (the first element is at position 1, not 0 like in some other programming languages).
For example, if you have (or create) a vector numbers and want to know what the 1st and 3rd elements are, you can use the code:

numbers <- c(10, 20, 30, 40, 50) # Adds the listed numbers to a vector and assigns it to the variable 'numbers'
print(numbers[1]) # Outputs the first element, here it is 10

[1] 10

print(numbers[3]) # Outputs the 3rd element, here it is 30

[1] 30

print(numbers[2:4]) # Outputs the elements in the range 2-4, here these are 20, 30 and 40

[1] 20 30 40


We can also extract multiple elements or select elements based on excluding other elements.

numbers[c(1, 3, 5)] # Gives the 1st, 3rd, and 5th elements

[1] 10 30 50

numbers[-1] # Gives all elements apart from the first element

[1] 20 30 40 50




Modifying vectors
You can update or replace vector elements.

Example: changing a value

numbers <- c(10, 20, 30, 40)
numbers[2] <- 25 # Change the second element
print(numbers) # Outputs: 10, 25, 30, 40

[1] 10 25 30 40




Example: adding new values

numbers <- c(numbers, 50, 60) # Append values
print(numbers) # Outputs: 10, 25, 30, 40, 50, 60

[1] 10 25 30 40 50 60




Example: removing values

numbers <- numbers[-3] # Remove the third element
print(numbers)

[1] 10 25 40 50 60





Performing operations on vectors
Vectors allow element-wise operations, meaning you can apply calculations to all elements at once.

Example: basic maths operations

x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)
y <- c(10, 20, 30, 40)
sum_x <- sum(x) # Sum of all elements
mean_y <- mean(y) # Mean of y
z <- x + y # Adds corresponding elements (1+10, 2+20, etc.)
print(sum_x) # Outputs: 10

[1] 10

print(mean_y) # Outputs: 25

[1] 25

print(z) # Outputs: 11, 22, 33, 44

[1] 11 22 33 44


Vectorised operations eliminate the need for loops, making calculations faster.



Logical operations on vectors
You can apply conditions to select elements.

Example: filtering values

ages <- c(25, 30, 35, 40)
ages_over_30 <- ages[ages > 30] # Extract values greater than 30
print(ages_over_30) # Outputs: 35, 40

[1] 35 40




Example: logical conditions

is_young <- ages < 35 # TRUE for ages < 35, FALSE otherwise
print(is_young) # Outputs: TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE

[1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE








WarningWatch out for missing values



If a vector contains NA, a condition such as ages > 30 gives NA for that element (R can’t know whether a missing age is over 30), and ages[ages > 30] then includes an NA in the result:

ages_with_missing <- c(25, 30, NA, 40)
ages_with_missing > 30

[1] FALSE FALSE    NA  TRUE

ages_with_missing[ages_with_missing > 30]

[1] NA 40


To keep only the values you know meet the condition, wrap the condition in which():

ages_with_missing[which(ages_with_missing > 30)]

[1] 40






Example: finding unique values

values <- c(1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4)
unique(values) # Outputs: 1, 2, 3, 4

[1] 1 2 3 4





Combining vectors

text: In session 2 you’ll start using the tidyverse, the family of R packages we use for the rest of the module. This page lets you try its three most important ideas in your browser before you meet them in RStudio: tables of data (tibbles), the pipe |>, and plotting with ggplot2.

title: Week 1, session 2: before the session
text:
1. A table of data
In R, a table of data is called a data frame; the tidyverse’s version is called a tibble. Each column holds one variable, and each row is one observation. R comes with some example datasets, and ToothGrowth is a biological one: the length of odontoblasts (the cells responsible for tooth growth) in 60 guinea pigs, each given one of three doses of vitamin C (0.5, 1 or 2 mg/day) as either orange juice (OJ) or ascorbic acid (VC).
glimpse() shows every column, its type and its first few values:








len and dose are numbers (<dbl>); supp is a factor, R’s way of storing a variable with a fixed set of categories.

title: Week 1, session 2: before the session
text:
2. The pipe and filter()
The pipe, |>, passes whatever is on its left into the function on its right. Read it as “and then”. filter() keeps only the rows that meet a condition:








This reads: “take ToothGrowth, and then keep the rows where dose equals 2”. Notice the two equals signs: == asks “is it equal?”, while a single = is used for naming arguments.
Predict before you run. What do you think happens with a single equals sign?














TipWhat happened?





R stops with an error, and the message suggests you meant ==. This is one of the commonest mistakes in the tidyverse, and one of the few where the error message tells you the fix directly. It’s always worth reading the whole error message.




Your turn
Keep only the guinea pigs that were given orange juice. The supplement is stored in the supp column, and the value you want is "OJ", in quotation marks because it is text.























NoteHint





The condition has the same shape as dose == 2: the column name, two equals signs, then the value: supp == ______.











TipSolution





ToothGrowth |> filter(supp == "OJ")

title: Week 1, session 2: before the session
text:
3. Choosing columns with select()
filter() chooses rows; select() chooses columns. Steps can be chained with more pipes, each one working on the result of the step before:









Your turn
Show only the len and dose columns, for all 60 animals.


















NoteHint





List the column names inside select(), separated by a comma. They don’t need quotation marks.











TipSolution





ToothGrowth |> select(len, dose)

title: Week 1, session 2: before the session
text:
4. A first plot
ggplot2 builds a plot in layers. You tell it the data, then use aes() to say which columns go on which axis, and then add a geom, the shape used to draw the data, with +:








factor(dose) tells ggplot to treat the three doses as three separate groups rather than as points on a number line.

Your turn
Points are fine, but a boxplot summarises each group more clearly. Replace the blank with the geom that draws boxplots. (Geoms all start geom_, and ggplot2 has one for most kinds of plot you can think of.)


















NoteHint





The geom for boxplots is called geom_boxplot.











TipSolution





ggplot(ToothGrowth, aes(x = factor(dose), y = len)) +
  geom_boxplot()










Warning+ between layers, not |>



The layers of a ggplot are joined with +. Using the pipe there instead is a very common slip, and ggplot’s error message will point it out.

Packages and data
This session uses the tidyverse, janitor (from session 1) and one new package, flextable, for making tables you can put in a Word document. Install flextable once, in the Console:

  clean_names() |>

    weight_3m = weight3m,

    sex = case_when(

text:
Summary statistics for one variable
For the numbers you’ll actually report, summarise() lets you choose exactly which statistics to calculate and what to call them:

dia |>
  summarise(
    n = sum(!is.na(hba1c_0m)),
    mean = mean(hba1c_0m, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(hba1c_0m, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(hba1c_0m, na.rm = TRUE),
    q1 = quantile(hba1c_0m, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    q3 = quantile(hba1c_0m, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    iqr = IQR(hba1c_0m, na.rm = TRUE),
    min = min(hba1c_0m, na.rm = TRUE),
    max = max(hba1c_0m, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 9
      n  mean    sd median    q1    q3   iqr   min   max
  <int> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1   232  8.36 0.862    8.4   7.8   8.9  1.10   6.2  11.1









Code
What it calculates




n = sum(!is.na(hba1c_0m))
The number of patients with a result. !is.na() is TRUE for every value that isn’t missing, and sum() counts the TRUEs.


mean = mean(...)
The mean: add up the values and divide by how many there are.


sd = sd(...)
The standard deviation: roughly, the typical distance of a value from the mean. In data that are roughly normally distributed, about two-thirds of values lie within one SD of the mean, and about 95% within two.


median = median(...)
The median: the middle value when they are sorted. Half the values are below it and half above.


q1, q3 = quantile(..., 0.25), quantile(..., 0.75)
The lower and upper quartiles: a quarter of the values lie below q1, and a quarter above q3.


iqr = IQR(...)
The interquartile range, q3 - q1: the range covered by the middle half of the values.


min, max
The smallest and largest values.


na.rm = TRUE
In every function: ignore the missing values. Without it, any NA makes the answer NA.



The words on the left of each = (n, mean, sd and so on) are just names for the columns of the result; you can call them whatever you like.
To get a single number rather than a table, you can also apply the function directly to one column, picked out with $:

mean(dia$hba1c_0m, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 8.359914



Mean or median?
The mean uses every value, so a few extreme values pull it towards them; the median only cares about the middle, so it hardly moves. When a variable is roughly symmetric, the two are close, and the mean and SD are the usual summary. When it is skewed, or has extreme values, they come apart, and the median and IQR describe a typical patient better. Baseline HbA1c is fairly symmetric (mean 8.36%, median 8.4%), so mean and SD are a fair summary. Biomarkers such as CRP, which are usually low but occasionally very high, are a classic case for the median and IQR; you’ll meet one in the workbook.






TipReport how many values each number is based on



Because na.rm = TRUE quietly drops missing values, always report n alongside a mean or median. Here, the baseline HbA1c summary is based on 232 of the 240 patients.

title: Guide to R 04: Descriptive statistics and graphs
text:
Summaries by group
Most studies compare groups. Put group_by() before summarise() and you get one row per group:

dia |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(
    n = sum(!is.na(hba1c_0m)),
    mean = mean(hba1c_0m, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(hba1c_0m, na.rm = TRUE),
    se = sd / sqrt(n),
    median = median(hba1c_0m, na.rm = TRUE),
    iqr = IQR(hba1c_0m, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 7
  group                   n  mean    sd     se median   iqr
  <fct>               <int> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 Usual care            120  8.44 0.870 0.0794   8.45  1.1 
2 Intensive lifestyle   112  8.27 0.848 0.0801   8.2   1.20









Code
What it does




group_by(group)
Splits the patients into the two treatment groups. Everything in summarise() is then calculated separately for each.


se = sd / sqrt(n)
The standard error of the mean: the SD divided by the square root of the number of values. Notice it uses the sd and n columns created on the lines above it, which summarise() allows.



The standard deviation and the standard error answer different questions, and they are often confused:

the SD describes the patients: how much individual HbA1c values vary around the mean;
the SE describes the mean: how precisely it has been estimated. If you repeated the study with new patients, the means would vary from study to study by about one SE. Because it is divided by √n, the SE gets smaller as the sample gets bigger, even though the patients don’t become any less variable.

Use the SD when you’re describing the sample, and the SE (or, better, a confidence interval, which you’ll meet in week 4) when you’re showing how precise a mean is.






WarningCount the values you used, not the rows



You’ll often see n() used to count each group. n() counts rows, including rows where the value is missing. For a standard error, you need the number of values the SD was actually calculated from, so use sum(!is.na(column)). With no missing values the two are the same; here they aren’t (120 of 124 usual-care patients have a baseline result).

title: Guide to R 04: Descriptive statistics and graphs
Guide to R 04: Descriptive statistics and graphs
text:
A table for a report
Console output isn’t suitable for a report. A table in a report should have readable column headings, a sensible number of decimal places, and only the information the reader needs. Build the numbers first, check them, and only then format them. Here is a typical “Table 1”, describing each group at baseline:

table1 <- dia |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    age = mean(age_yrs),
    female = 100 * mean(sex == "Female"),
    smokers = 100 * mean(smoker == "Yes"),
    hba1c = mean(hba1c_0m, na.rm = TRUE),
    weight = mean(weight_0m)
  )

table1

# A tibble: 2 × 7
  group                   n   age female smokers hba1c weight
  <fct>               <int> <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
1 Usual care            124  58.2   57.3    33.1  8.44   89.3
2 Intensive lifestyle   116  57.5   45.7    35.3  8.27   90.0


mean(sex == "Female") is a useful trick: sex == "Female" is TRUE or FALSE for each patient, and the mean of TRUEs and FALSEs is the proportion that are TRUE. Multiplying by 100 gives a percentage. (n() is fine here because every patient counts, whatever they’re missing.)
The flextable package turns a tibble into a formatted table:

table1 |>
  flextable() |>
  set_header_labels(
    group = "Group",
    n = "n",
    age = "Mean age (years)",
    female = "Female (%)",
    smokers = "Smokers (%)",
    hba1c = "Mean HbA1c (%)",
    weight = "Mean weight (kg)"
  ) |>
  colformat_double(digits = 1) |>
  autofit()

GroupnMean age (years)Female (%)Smokers (%)Mean HbA1c (%)Mean weight (kg)Usual care12458.257.333.18.489.3Intensive lifestyle11657.545.735.38.390.0









Code
What it does




flextable()
Turns the tibble into a flextable object.


set_header_labels(...)
Replaces each column name with a readable heading: column name on the left of =, heading on the right.


colformat_double(digits = 1)
Shows every decimal number to one decimal place. (Only the display changes; the numbers underneath are unchanged.)


autofit()
Sizes the columns to fit their contents.



To save the table as a Word document, store it with <-, then use save_as_docx():

table1_ft <- table1 |>
  flextable() |>
  set_header_labels(group = "Group", age = "Mean age (years)") |>
  colformat_double(digits = 1) |>
  autofit()

save_as_docx(table1_ft, path = "table1.docx")

The file is saved in your project folder. Open it in Word and copy the table into your report.

title: Guide to R 04: Descriptive statistics and graphs
text:
Checking for outliers
An outlier is a value that is unusually far from the rest. Outliers can be genuine (one patient really does have a very high CRP), or they can be errors (a typing slip, or a missing-value code you haven’t found yet). The usual rule of thumb, and the one boxplots use, is that a value is a potential outlier if it is more than 1.5 × IQR above the upper quartile or below the lower quartile. You can find those values with filter():

dia |>
  filter(hba1c_0m > quantile(hba1c_0m, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) + 1.5 * IQR(hba1c_0m, na.rm = TRUE) |
         hba1c_0m < quantile(hba1c_0m, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE) - 1.5 * IQR(hba1c_0m, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  select(patient_id, group, hba1c_0m)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  patient_id group               hba1c_0m
  <chr>      <fct>                  <dbl>
1 PT118      Usual care              11.1
2 PT119      Intensive lifestyle     10.7
3 PT144      Usual care              10.7


Three patients have baseline HbA1c values above the cut-off (here, 10.55%). An HbA1c of 11% is high but entirely plausible in someone with poorly controlled diabetes, so these are almost certainly real. Being an outlier is not a reason to delete a value. Check whether it is possible; if it is, keep it, and choose summaries (medians) and methods that aren’t thrown by it. If it is impossible, treat it as an error, set it to NA, and report what you did.

text:
Choosing the right graph








Graph
Use it to show
Example question for the diabetes data




Histogram
The distribution of one continuous variable
What does the spread of baseline HbA1c look like?


Boxplot
The distribution of a continuous variable in several groups
How does HbA1c at 6 months differ between the groups?


Scatter plot
The relationship between two continuous variables
Do patients who lose more weight see bigger falls in HbA1c?


Bar chart
Counts of a categorical variable (or, with care, group means)
How many smokers are there in each group?

title: Guide to R 04: Descriptive statistics and graphs
text:
How ggplot2 builds a graph
ggplot2 is the most widely used R package for graphs, and part of the tidyverse. It is based on the grammar of graphics, which breaks every graph into the same few parts:

the data: ggplot(dia, ...);
the aesthetic mappings, aes(): which column goes on the x axis, which on the y, which controls colour or fill;
one or more geoms: the marks that represent the data (bars, boxes, points, lines); and
everything else, added in layers with +: labels (labs()), colour scales, themes and annotations.

Anything inside aes() is linked to a column, so it changes with the data: aes(colour = group) colours each point by its group. Anything outside aes() is a fixed setting: colour = "#753bbd" makes every point the same purple. Putting a fixed setting inside aes() by mistake (aes(colour = "purple")) gives a strange legend and the wrong colour, because ggplot treats the word “purple” as a category.
The ggplot2 website lists every geom, scale and theme, with examples.

title: Guide to R 04: Descriptive statistics and graphs
text:
Histograms
A histogram divides the range of a variable into bins and draws a bar for the number of values in each. It shows the shape of the distribution:

ggplot(dia, aes(x = hba1c_0m)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, fill = "#753bbd", colour = "white") +
  labs(title = "Baseline HbA1c",
       x = "HbA1c (%)",
       y = "Number of patients") +
  theme_minimal()

Warning: Removed 8 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_bin()`).
















Code
What it does




ggplot(dia, aes(x = hba1c_0m))
Uses dia, with baseline HbA1c on the x axis. A histogram needs only an x; ggplot counts the y for you.


geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, ...)
Draws the histogram, with each bar covering 0.25 percentage points of HbA1c.


fill = "#753bbd", colour = "white"
Fixed settings, outside aes(): purple bars with a white outline, so neighbouring bars are easy to tell apart.


labs(...)
The title and axis labels. Always give the units.


theme_minimal()
A clean theme with a white background.



ggplot warns that it has removed 8 rows: those are the patients with a missing result, which can’t be plotted. The warning is worth reading, because it tells you how many values the plot is based on.
The distribution is roughly symmetric, centred on about 8.4%, with three values trailing off to the right (the outliers found above). The bin width matters: too wide and the shape disappears into a few blocks, too narrow and it becomes spiky noise. Try a few values. To compare groups, facet_wrap() draws one panel per group, on the same axes:

ggplot(dia, aes(x = hba1c_6m)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, fill = "#753bbd", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ group, ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "HbA1c at 6 months",
       x = "HbA1c (%)",
       y = "Number of patients") +
  theme_minimal()

Warning: Removed 9 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_bin()`).









facet_wrap(~ group, ncol = 1) splits the plot by group and stacks the panels in one column (~ means “by”), so the two distributions line up on the same scale. The intensive lifestyle group’s distribution sits clearly to the left.

title: Guide to R 04: Descriptive statistics and graphs
text:
Boxplots
A boxplot summarises a distribution in five numbers: the line in the box is the median, the box runs from the lower to the upper quartile (so its height is the IQR), the whiskers reach the most extreme values within 1.5 × IQR of the box, and anything beyond that is drawn as a separate point (a potential outlier). Boxplots are ideal for comparing groups:

ggplot(dia, aes(x = group, y = hba1c_6m, fill = group)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Usual care" = "#b48fe0",
                               "Intensive lifestyle" = "#4b2479")) +
  labs(title = "HbA1c at 6 months",
       x = NULL,
       y = "HbA1c (%)") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

Warning: Removed 9 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_boxplot()`).
















Code
What it does




aes(x = group, y = hba1c_6m, fill = group)
One box per group on the x axis, HbA1c on the y axis, and each box filled according to its group.


geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.8)
Draws the boxes; alpha sets the transparency, from 0 (invisible) to 1 (solid).


scale_fill_manual(values = ...)
Chooses the fill colour for each group by name. The names must match the factor levels exactly, including capitals.


x = NULL
Removes the x-axis title, because the group names already say everything.


theme_classic()
A theme with axis lines and no grid.


theme(legend.position = "none")
Removes the legend, which would only repeat the x axis.



A boxplot hides how many patients are in each group and what the individual values look like. Adding the points themselves, spread sideways a little so they don’t sit on top of each other, shows both:

ggplot(dia, aes(x = group, y = hba1c_6m, fill = group)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6, colour = "#4b2479") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Usual care" = "#b48fe0",
                               "Intensive lifestyle" = "#4b2479")) +
  labs(title = "HbA1c at 6 months", x = NULL, y = "HbA1c (%)") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

Warning: Removed 9 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_boxplot()`).


Warning: Removed 9 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).









outlier.shape = NA stops the boxplot drawing its own outlier points, because the jittered points already include them. geom_jitter(width = 0.15) moves each point a small random distance left or right (never up or down, so the values aren’t changed).

title: Guide to R 04: Descriptive statistics and graphs
text:
Scatter plots
A scatter plot shows the relationship between two continuous variables, one point per patient. Here is each patient’s change in weight against their change in HbA1c over the six months, calculated with mutate() first:

dia <- dia |>
  mutate(
    weight_change = weight_6m - weight_0m,
    hba1c_change = hba1c_6m - hba1c_0m
  )

ggplot(dia, aes(x = weight_change, y = hba1c_change)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, colour = "#753bbd") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "#4b2479") +
  labs(title = "Change in weight and HbA1c over six months",
       x = "Change in weight (kg)",
       y = "Change in HbA1c (percentage points)") +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'


Warning: Removed 17 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_smooth()`).


Warning: Removed 17 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).
















Code
What it does




weight_change = weight_6m - weight_0m
A new column: each patient’s weight at 6 months minus their weight at baseline. Negative values mean weight was lost.


geom_point(alpha = 0.6, ...)
One point per patient, slightly transparent, so overlapping points show up darker.


geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)
Adds the straight line that best fits the points (lm is short for linear model; you’ll meet it properly in week 5). se = FALSE hides the shaded band around the line.



(The warning about removed rows refers to the 17 patients missing either HbA1c result, whose change can’t be calculated.) Overall, patients who lost more weight tended to have bigger falls in HbA1c. But look what happens when the two groups are coloured differently, with a line for each:

ggplot(dia, aes(x = weight_change, y = hba1c_change, colour = group)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Usual care" = "#b48fe0",
                                 "Intensive lifestyle" = "#4b2479")) +
  labs(title = "Change in weight and HbA1c over six months",
       x = "Change in weight (kg)",
       y = "Change in HbA1c (percentage points)",
       colour = "Group") +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'


Warning: Removed 17 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_smooth()`).


Warning: Removed 17 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).









Within each group, the lines are almost flat: there is little sign that the patients who lost the most weight had the biggest falls in HbA1c. The overall trend in the first plot came almost entirely from the difference between the groups: the lifestyle group lost more weight and had bigger falls in HbA1c. A relationship across a whole sample can disappear, or even reverse, within its subgroups, which is why it is always worth colouring or splitting a scatter plot by the groups in your study.

title: Guide to R 04: Descriptive statistics and graphs
text:
Bar charts

Bars for counts
geom_bar() counts the rows in each category and draws a bar for each count. Use it for categorical variables:

ggplot(dia, aes(x = group, fill = smoker)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("No" = "#b48fe0", "Yes" = "#4b2479")) +
  labs(title = "Smoking status by group",
       x = NULL, y = "Number of patients", fill = "Smoker") +
  theme_light()








position = "dodge" puts the bars for each smoking status side by side; without it, they would be stacked on top of each other. Because the groups are different sizes, percentages (see above) are often fairer to compare than counts.


Bars for means, with error bars
Bar charts are also widely used to show group means, with error bars for the standard error. To draw one, calculate the summary first, then plot the summary with geom_col(), which draws bars at the heights you give it:

hba1c_6m_summary <- dia |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(
    n = sum(!is.na(hba1c_6m)),
    mean = mean(hba1c_6m, na.rm = TRUE),
    se = sd(hba1c_6m, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n)
  )

ggplot(hba1c_6m_summary, aes(x = group, y = mean, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se), width = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Usual care" = "#b48fe0",
                               "Intensive lifestyle" = "#4b2479")) +
  labs(title = "Mean HbA1c at 6 months",
       x = NULL, y = "Mean HbA1c (%) ± SE") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")















Code
What it does




geom_col(width = 0.6)
Draws one bar per row of the summary, with its height taken from mean.


geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se), width = 0.2)
Draws an error bar from one SE below the mean to one SE above it; width sets the width of the horizontal ends.


y = "Mean HbA1c (%) ± SE"
Always say what the error bars show: SD, SE and confidence intervals all look the same on a plot.









WarningThink twice before using bars for means



Compare this chart with the boxplots above. The bar chart shows two numbers and two error bars; the boxplot shows the whole distribution, including the large overlap between the groups. Bars also start at zero, which squashes differences when, as with HbA1c, no patient’s value is anywhere near zero. Many journals now discourage bar charts of means for continuous data. Prefer a boxplot, or points with the mean marked, and keep bar charts for counts.

title: Guide to R 04: Descriptive statistics and graphs
text:
Line graphs
A line graph is the natural way to show change over time. It needs data in long format, with the time variable in one column. Here are the mean and standard error at each timepoint in each group, from hba1c_long:

hba1c_summary <- hba1c_long |>
  group_by(group, timepoint) |>
  summarise(
    n = sum(!is.na(hba1c)),
    mean = mean(hba1c, na.rm = TRUE),
    se = sd(hba1c, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

`summarise()` has regrouped the output.
ℹ Summaries were computed grouped by group and timepoint.
ℹ Output is grouped by group.
ℹ Use `summarise(.groups = "drop_last")` to silence this message.
ℹ Use `summarise(.by = c(group, timepoint))` for per-operation grouping
  (`?dplyr::dplyr_by`) instead.

ggplot(hba1c_summary, aes(x = timepoint, y = mean, colour = group, group = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se), width = 0.1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Usual care" = "#b48fe0",
                                 "Intensive lifestyle" = "#4b2479")) +
  labs(title = "Mean HbA1c over six months",
       x = NULL, y = "Mean HbA1c (%) ± SE", colour = "Group") +
  theme_bw()















Code
What it does




group = group
Tells ggplot which points to join into each line. With a factor on the x axis, ggplot can’t work this out for itself.


geom_line(linewidth = 1)
Joins the points. (In older code you’ll see size = 1 for lines; current versions of ggplot2 use linewidth.)


geom_errorbar(...)
Error bars, exactly as in the bar chart.


theme_bw()
A black-and-white theme with a light grid.



The error bars are small because there are over 100 patients at each point; compare them with the spread of the individual values in the boxplots.

title: Guide to R 04: Descriptive statistics and graphs
text:
Colours and themes
Colours can be given by name (R knows over 600, from "black" to "mediumorchid") or, more precisely, by hex code: a # followed by six characters giving the amounts of red, green and blue. The purples used in this guide are:








Colour
Hex code
Used for




Dark purple
#4b2479
Intensive lifestyle; lines and text


Purple
#753bbd
Single-colour plots


Light purple
#b48fe0
Usual care



Shades of one colour that differ a lot in lightness, like these, stay distinguishable when printed in black and white and for readers with colour-vision deficiencies, which red-and-green pairs don’t. Use scale_fill_manual() for anything drawn with fill (bars, boxes, histograms) and scale_colour_manual() for anything drawn with colour (points, lines).
A theme controls everything that isn’t data: background, grid lines, fonts. The built-in themes include theme_minimal(), theme_classic(), theme_bw() and theme_light(), and theme() changes individual elements. For example, theme(legend.position = "bottom") moves the legend, and theme(text = element_text(size = 14)) makes all the text bigger. Type ?theme in the Console for the full list.

title: Guide to R 04: Descriptive statistics and graphs
text:
Annotations
Annotations point the reader to what matters. Lines mark thresholds, text and arrows label features, and shaded areas mark ranges.

Reference lines
geom_hline() draws a horizontal line, and geom_vline() a vertical one. Here, the mean HbA1c plot with a line at 7% (53 mmol/mol), a commonly used treatment target, and a text label:

ggplot(hba1c_summary, aes(x = timepoint, y = mean, colour = group, group = group)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 7, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.6, y = 7.08, label = "7% treatment target",
           hjust = 0, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Usual care" = "#b48fe0",
                                 "Intensive lifestyle" = "#4b2479")) +
  labs(title = "Mean HbA1c over six months",
       x = NULL, y = "Mean HbA1c (%)", colour = "Group") +
  theme_bw()















Code
What it does




geom_hline(yintercept = 7, linetype = "dashed", ...)
A dashed horizontal line at y = 7. It comes first so the data are drawn on top of it.


annotate("text", x = 0.6, y = 7.08, label = ..., hjust = 0)
Writes the label at the position given. On a factor axis the categories sit at positions 1, 2, 3, …, so x = 0.6 is just left of “Baseline”. hjust = 0 lines up the start of the text with that position. With a factor on the x axis, put annotate() after the geoms that use the factor, or ggplot gets confused about the type of axis.





Arrows and labels
annotate("segment") draws a line between two points; adding arrow = arrow() turns it into an arrow. Here, pointing out the three high baseline values:

ggplot(dia, aes(x = hba1c_0m)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, fill = "#753bbd", colour = "white") +
  annotate("segment", x = 10.3, xend = 10.8, y = 14, yend = 4,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "inches")), colour = "#4b2479") +
  annotate("text", x = 10.3, y = 16, label = "Three unusually high values",
           colour = "#4b2479", fontface = "bold") +
  labs(title = "Baseline HbA1c", x = "HbA1c (%)", y = "Number of patients") +
  theme_minimal()

Warning: Removed 8 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_bin()`).









The arrow runs from (x, y) to (xend, yend), in the units of the axes. arrow(length = unit(0.15, "inches")) sets the size of the arrowhead. Expect to adjust the positions by trial and error.


Shaded areas
annotate("rect") draws a rectangle, from xmin to xmax and from ymin to ymax; -Inf and Inf stretch it to the edges of the plot. Here, shading the HbA1c values below the 7% target on the 6-month histograms. The rectangle comes before the histogram, so the bars are drawn on top of it, and it appears in both panels:

ggplot(dia, aes(x = hba1c_6m)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = 7, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#e4d8f4", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, fill = "#753bbd", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ group, ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "HbA1c at 6 months",
       subtitle = "Shaded area: below the 7% treatment target",
       x = "HbA1c (%)", y = "Number of patients") +
  theme_minimal()

Warning: Removed 9 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_bin()`).









At 6 months, 74 of the 110 patients with a result in the intensive lifestyle group are below the target, compared with 26 of 121 in usual care.






Notep-values and significance stars



Plots in papers often have p-values or stars (*, **, ***) above the groups. A p-value comes from a statistical test, so we’ll add them in week 4, when you meet t-tests. Until then, describe, don’t test.

Saving graphs
Run ggsave() straight after the plot you want to save. The file type comes from the ending of the file name, and the path is relative to the project folder (create a figures folder in the Files pane first):

ggsave("figures/hba1c_over_time.png", width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300) # an image file
ggsave("figures/hba1c_over_time.pdf", width = 8, height = 5) # a PDF, which stays sharp at any size








Code
What it does




ggsave("figures/....png", ...)
Saves the most recent plot. Change the file name for each plot, or the next one will overwrite it.


width = 8, height = 5
The size in inches. Text sizes are fixed, so a smaller size makes the text look bigger.


dpi = 300
The resolution of an image file, in dots per inch. 300 is the usual standard for print and publication.



You can also copy a plot from the Plots pane (Export › Copy to Clipboard) and paste it into Word, but ggsave() gives you control over the size and resolution, and saves the same plot every time the code runs.

title: Week 2, session 1: before the session
text: Real data is rarely ready to analyse. The same category gets typed three different ways, numbers arrive with units stuck to them, someone writes 999 to mean “no result”, and the measurements are laid out in whatever shape suited the spreadsheet rather than the analysis. In session 1 you’ll take a messy dataset from a diabetes trial and get it into shape. This page introduces the four tools you’ll use most:

title: Week 2, session 1: before the session
text:
1. Finding problems with count()
The box above created a tibble called clinic: eight patients, their sex, whether they smoke, and a fasting glucose result in mmol/L. Print it to see what’s inside:








With eight rows you can spot the problems by eye. With 800 you can’t, so you need a tool that shows you every different value in a column. That tool is count(). It counts how many rows have each value:








R treats every distinct spelling as a separate category, so this one column, which ought to have two categories, has four. Nothing has gone wrong in R. The data was recorded inconsistently, and count() has made that visible.

Your turn
Use count() to find out how many different ways smoking status has been recorded.






















NoteHint





It’s exactly like clinic |> count(sex), with a different column name.











TipSolution





clinic |> count(smoker)
Six codes for two answers: Y, Yes and 1 all mean “smoker”; N, No and 0 all mean “non-smoker”.

title: Week 2, session 1: before the session
text:
2. Fixing categories with case_when()
case_when() goes inside mutate() and works through a list of rules, one per line. Each rule has a condition on the left of a tilde, ~, and the value to use on the right. Read the ~ as “then”:








The first rule reads: “if sex is one of "F" or "female", then use "Female"”. %in% asks whether a value appears anywhere in the list that follows. Ending the code with count() checks that the fix worked: two categories, and the counts add up to eight.
Any value that doesn’t match a rule becomes NA (missing). That’s deliberate: if a new spelling turns up, you’ll see an NA in your count() rather than a wrong answer slipping through silently.

Your turn
Recode smoker so that it contains only "Yes" and "No". Fill in the two lists of codes (use the output of Exercise 1, and remember that text values need quotation marks).


















NoteHint





The first list needs the three codes that mean “smoker”, each in quotation marks and separated by commas: c("Y", "Yes", "1"). Notice that "1" needs quotation marks too, because the column is text.











TipSolution





clinic |>
  mutate(
    smoker = case_when(
      smoker %in% c("Y", "Yes", "1") ~ "Yes",
      smoker %in% c("N", "No", "0") ~ "No"
    )
  ) |>
  count(smoker)

title: Week 2, session 1: before the session
section: 3. Missing values, and codes that mean “missing”
text:
3. Missing values, and codes that mean “missing”
Two of the glucose results are -99 and 999. Neither is a possible fasting glucose; in this dataset they are codes that whoever entered the data used to mean “no result”. R can’t know that, so it treats them as real numbers. Look what that does to the mean:








A mean fasting glucose of 117 mmol/L is impossible: a normal value is roughly 4 to 6. (clinic$glucose means “the glucose column of clinic”.) R’s own symbol for a missing value is NA, so the first job is to swap the codes for NA. if_else() does this: if the value is one of the codes, use NA, otherwise keep the value as it is.








Now try the mean again:








The answer is NA. That’s R being careful, not awkward: if some values are unknown, then strictly speaking the mean is unknown too. To get the mean of the values you do have, you have to say so, with na.rm = TRUE (“NA remove: yes”).

Your turn
Calculate the mean glucose of the six patients with a real result.





















NoteHint





na.rm is an argument of mean(), so it goes inside the brackets of mean(), after glucose and a comma.











TipSolution





clinic |> summarise(mean_glucose = mean(glucose, na.rm = TRUE))










WarningRemoving missing values is a decision



na.rm = TRUE means the mean is based on six patients, not eight. That’s usually what you want, but it is a choice, and in a report you should say how many values each result is based on. In session 1 you’ll see why it matters which patients are missing.

title: Week 2, session 1: before the session
text:
4. Changing shape with pivot_longer()
Here are three patients’ systolic blood pressures (mmHg), measured at the start of a study and again after 6 months:








This is wide format: one row per patient, with the timepoints spread across the columns. It’s easy to read, but the timepoint (a variable) is hidden in the column names, and R’s plotting and summary functions can’t get at it there. Long format has one row per patient per timepoint, with the timepoint in a column of its own. pivot_longer() makes the change:









cols lists the columns to stack;
names_to names the new column that will hold the old column names; and
values_to names the new column that will hold the values.

Three patients × two timepoints = six rows.

Your turn
Here are the same three patients’ weights (kg) at baseline, 3 months and 6 months. Turn the table into long format, with a column called timepoint and a column called weight.





















NoteHint





cols = c(weight_0m, weight_3m, weight_6m): column names need no quotation marks here, but the new column names after names_to and values_to do, because they don’t exist yet.











TipSolution





weight_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(weight_0m, weight_3m, weight_6m),
    names_to = "timepoint",
    values_to = "weight"
  )

title: Week 2, session 1: before the session
text:
Before you come in
You’re ready for session 1 if you can:

use count() to see every value in a column, and explain why one category can show up as several;
use case_when() inside mutate() to recode values, and check the result with count();
explain what NA is, why mean() returns NA when a value is missing, and what na.rm = TRUE does; and
